name: Endeis

Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Erigone

name: Ithome

name: Laophonte

name: Megamede

source: Written Ἐπιπολή / Ἐπιπολλά. Strictly Epipolē. A daughter of Trachion, of Carystus in Euboea (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Eriphanis
source: Written Ἠριφανίς. Strictly Ēriphanis. A melic poetess, and author of erotic poetry (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Eurymede
source: Written Εὐρυμήδη. Strictly Eurymēdē. The name of two mythical personages. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Galba
source: Written Γάλβα. The name of a patrician family of the Sulpicia gens. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Gerana
source: Written Γεράνα. A Pygmean woman, and wife of their king, Nicodamas, by whom she became the mother of Mopsus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hagno
source: Written Ἁγνώ. Strictly Hagnō. An Arcadian nymph, who is said to have brought up Zeus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Halosydne
source: Written Ἁλοσύδνη. Strictly Halosydnē. That is, "the seafed," or the sea born goddess, occurs as a surname of Amiphitrite and Thetys. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Harpinna
source: Written Ἅρπιννα. A daughter of Asopus, from whom the town of Harpina or Harpinna in Elis was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hecale
source: Written Ἑκάλη. Strictly Hekalē. A poor old woman, who hospitably received into her house Theseus, when he had gone out for the purpose of killing the Marathonian bull (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hedyle
source: Written Ἡδύλη. Strictly Hēdylē. An Iambic poetess, daughter of Moschine the Athenian, and mother of HEDYLUS. She wrote a poem entitled Ζκύλλη , from which a passage is cite (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hegemone
source: Written Ἡγεμόνη. Strictly Hēgemonē. That is, the leader or ruler, is the name of one of the Athenian Charites (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hellotia
source: Written Ἐλλωτία / Ἑλλωτίς. Strictly Ellōtia. Or HELLO'TIS, a surname of Athena at Corinth (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hemeresia
source: Written Ἡμερησία. Strictly Hēmerēsia. I.e. the soothing goddess, a surname of Artemis, under which she was worshipped at the well Lusi, in Arcadia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hesychia
source: Written Ἡσυχία. Strictly Hēsykhia. The personification of tranquillity and peace, is called a daughter of Dice, that is, Justice. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Historis
source: Written Ἱστορίς. A daughter of Teiresias, and engaged in the service of Alcmene (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hygiea
source: Written Ὑγίεια. Strictly Hygieia. Also called Hygea or Hygia, the goddess of health, and a daughter of Asclepius. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hymnia
source: Written Ὑμνία. A surname of Artemis, under which she was worshipped throughout Arcadia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Iasonia
source: Written Ἰασονία. A surname of Athena at Cyzicus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Iliona
source: Written Ἰλίωνα. Strictly Iliōna. A daughter of Priam and Hecabe, is not mentioned by the earlier poets and mythographers, but the later ones relate of her the following stor (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Iocaste
source: Written Ἰοκάστη. Strictly Iokastē. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Iodamea
source: Written Ἰοδάμεια. Strictly Iodameia. A priestess of Athena Itonia, who once, as she entered the sanctuary of the goddess by night, was changed into a block of stone on seeing th (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Iophossa
source: Written Ἰοφῶσσα. Strictly Iophōssa. A daughter of Aeetes, commonly called Chalciope. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Iynx
source: Written Ἴυγξ. Strictly Iugx. A daughter of Peitho and Pan, or of Echo (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Laocoosa
source: Written Λαοκόωσα. Strictly Laokoōsa. The wife of Aphareus, and mother of Idas. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Laonome
source: Written Λαονόμν. Strictly Laonomn. The wife of Alcaeus, and mother of Amphitryo. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Laphria
source: Written Λαφραία. Strictly Laphraia. A surname of Artemis among the Calydonians, from whom the worship of the goddess was introduced at Naupactus and Patrae, in Achaia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Larymna
source: Written Λάρυμνα. A daughter of Cynus, from whom the Boeotian town of Lary is said to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Leprea
source: Written Λέπρεα. A daughter of Pyrgeus, from whom the town of Lepreum, in the south of Elis, was said to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lochea
source: Written Λοχεία. Strictly Lokheia. The protectress of women in childbed, occurs as a surname of Artemis. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Longatis
source: Written Λογγᾶτις. A surname of Athena (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Loxo
source: Written Λοξώ. Strictly Loxō. A daughter of Boreas, one of the Hyperborean maidens, who brought the worship of Artemis to Delos, whence it is also used as a surname of Ar (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lygodesma
source: Written Λυγοδέσμα. A surname of Artemis whose statue had been found by the brothers Astrabacus and Alopecus under a bush of willows, by which it was surrounded (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lysizona
source: Written Λυσιζώνη. Strictly Lysizōnē. I. e. the goddess who loosens the girdle, is a surname of Artemis and Eileithyia, who were worshipped under this name at Athens. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Magarsia
source: Written Μαγαρσία / Μαγαρσις. A surname of Athena, derived from Magarsos, a Cilician town near the mouth of the river Pyramus, where the goddess had a sanctuary. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mestra
source: Written Μήστρα. Strictly Mēstra. A daughter of Erysichthon, and granddaughter of Triopas (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Molpadia
source: Written Μολπαδία. An Amazon, who was said to have killed Antiope, another Amazon, and was afterwards slain herself by Theseus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mothone
source: Written Μοθώνη. Strictly Mothōnē. A daughter of Oeneus, from whom the town of Mothone was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Nedusia
source: Written Νεδουσία. Strictly Nedousia. A surname of Athena, under which she had a sanctuary on the river Nedon, and another at Poieessa in the island of Cos (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Nonacris
source: Written Νωνακρίς. Strictly Nōnakris. The wife of Lycaon, from whom the town of Nonacris in Arcadia was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ocalea
source: Written Ὠκάλεια. Strictly Ōkaleia. A daughter of Mantineus, and wife of Abas, by whom she became the mother of Acrisius and Proetus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ogoa
source: Written Ὀγώα. Strictly Ogōa. The Carian name of Zeus at Mysala, in whose temple a sea-wave was seen from time to time. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Orthia
source: Written Ὀρθωσία. Strictly Orthōsia. A surname of the Artemis who is also called Iphigeneia or Lygodesma, and must be regarded as the goddess of the moon (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Paphia
source: Written Παφία. A surname of Aphrodite, derived from the celebrated temple of the goddess at Paphos in Cyprus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Paramone
source: Written Παραμόνη / Παραμόνα. Strictly Paramonē. Borne by 99 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 323 BC to 600 AD. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Pelarge
source: Written Πελαργή. Strictly Pelargē. The daughter of Potneus, and wife of Isthmiades, was said to have instituted the orgies of the Boeotian Cabeiri. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pepromene
source: Written Πεπρωμένη. Strictly Peprōmenē. Namely etopa, that is, the share destined by fate, occurs also as a proper name in the same sense as Moira or Fate. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Perimele
source: Written Περιμήλη. Strictly Perimēlē. The name of three mythical personages, the first a daughter of Hippodamas (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Perso
source: Written Περσώ. Strictly Persō. One of the Graeae. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phigalia
source: Written Φιγαλία. A Dryad, from whom the town of Phigalia was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phillyra
source: Written Φίλλυρα. According to some accounts, the mother of Hypseus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phranza
source: Written Φραντζῆ / Φραντζῆς. Strictly Phrantzē. Or PHRANZES, the last and one of the most important Byzantine historians, was born in A. D. 1401 , and was appointed chamberlain to the empe (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Physadea
source: Written Φυσάδεια. Strictly Physadeia. A daughter of Danaus, from whom the well of Physadeia near Argos, was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pitanatis
source: Written Πιτανᾶτις. A surname of Artemis, derived from the little town of Pitana in Laconia, where she had a temple. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Proclea
source: Written Πρόκλεια. Strictly Prokleia. A daughter of Laomedon, and the wife of Cycnus, by whom she became the another of Tennes and Hemithea. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Rhamnusia
source: Written Ῥαμνουσία. Strictly Rhamnousia. A surname of Nemesis, who had a celebrated temple at Rhamnus in Attica. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Saitis
source: Written Σαῖτις. A surname of Athena, under which she had a sanctuary on Mount Pontinus, near Lerna in Argolis. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Saronis
source: Written Σαρωνίς. Strictly Sarōnis. A surname of Artemis at Troezene, where an annual festival was celebrated in honour of her under the name of Saronia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Segesta
source: Written Σεγέστη. Strictly Segestē. The Trojan Phoenodamas had three daughters (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sito
source: Written Σιτώ. Strictly Sitō. A surname of Demeter, describing her as the giver of food or corn. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Stilbe
source: Written Στίλβη. Strictly Stilbē. A daughter of Peneius and Creusa, became by Apollo the mother of Lapithus and Centaurus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Theisoa
source: Written Θεισόα. One of the nymphs who brought up the infant Zeus, was worshipped at Theisoa in Arcadia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Therapne
source: Written Θεράπνη. Strictly Therapnē. A daughter of Lelex and Peridia, from which the town of Therapne in Laconia derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Thesmia
source: Written Θεσμία / Θεσμοφόρος. Or THESMO'PHOROS, that is, " the law-giver," a surname of Demeter and Persephone, in honour of whom the Thesmophoria were celebrated at Athe (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Thuro
source: Written Θουρώ. Strictly Thourō. A daughter of Phylas, became by Apollo the mother of Chaeron, the founder of Thurium. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tilphusa
source: Written Τιλφοῦσα. Strictly Tilphousa. The nymph of the well Tilphusa in Boeotia, which was sacred to Apollo. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tithorea
source: Written Τιθορέα. A nymph of Mount Parnassus, from whom the town of Tithorea, previously called Neon, was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Trigonea
source: Written Τριγόνεια / Τριτυγένεια. Strictly Trigoneia. Or TRITOGENEIA, a daughter of Aeolus, and the wife of Minyas, or according to others, the mother of Minyas by Poseidon. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Trophon

name: Upis

name: Amythaon

name: Assaracus

name: Astynous

name: Borus

name: Hesiodus

name: Ithacus

name: Mermerus

name: Molus

name: Mulius
source: Written Μούλιος. Strictly Moulios. The son-in-law of Augeas, and husband of Agamede, was slain by Nestor. (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 11.739; Odyssey 18.423. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Naubolus

name: Nycteus

name: Salmoneus

name: Thalpius

source: Written Μολης / Μόλης. Strictly Molēs. Borne by 111 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Thraseas
source: Written Θρασείας / Θρασέας. Borne by 78 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 400 BC to 310 AD. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Dioclidas
source: Written Διοκλίδας / Διοκλείδας. Strictly Diokleidas. Borne by 36 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 499 BC to 310 AD. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Tatias
source: Written Τατιάς / Τατιας / Τατίας. Borne by 108 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 350 BC to 301 BC. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Temon
source: Written Τέμων. Strictly Temōn. Borne by 2 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 998 BC to 137 AD. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Xystus
source: Written Ξύστος. Strictly Xystos. Borne by 25 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Chryserus
source: Written Χρυσέρως. Strictly Khryserōs. Borne by 102 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Trocondas
source: Written Τροκονδας / Τροκόνδας. Strictly Trokondas. Borne by 101 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 323 BC to 310 AD. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Boiscus
source: Written Βοΐσκος. Strictly Boiskos. Borne by 100 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Abellio
source: Written Ἀβέλιος. Strictly Abelios. Is the name of a divinity found in inscriptions which were discovered at Comminges in France. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Abiares
source: Written Ἀβισάρης. Strictly Abisarēs. Or ABI'SSARES, called Embisarus by Diodorus, an Indian king beyond the river Hydaspes, whose territory lay in the mountains, sent embassies  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Abitianus
source: Written Ἀβιτζιανός. Strictly Abitzianos. The author of a Greek treatise De Urinis inserted in the second volume of Ideler's Physici et Medici Graeci Minores, Berol (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Abulites
source: Written Ἀβουλίτης. Strictly Aboulitēs. The satrap of Susiana, surrendered Susa to Alexander , when the latter approached the city (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Acacus
source: Written Ἄκακος. Strictly Akakos. A son of Lycaon and king of Acacesium in Arcadia, of which he was believed to be the founder. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Acoris
source: Written Ἄκορις. Strictly Akoris. King of Egypt, entered into alliance with Evagoras, king of Cyprus, against their common enemy Artaxerxes, king of Persia, about B. C. 385 , (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Actisanes
source: Written Ἀκτισάνης. Strictly Aktisanēs. A king of Ethiopia, who conquered Egypt and governed it with justice (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Actuarius
source: Written Ἀκτουάριος. Strictly Aktouarios. The surname by which an ancient Greek physician, whose real name was Joannes, is commonly known (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Adiatorix
source: Written Ἀδιατόριξ. Son of a tetrarch in Galatia, belonged to Antony's party, and killed all the Romans in Heracleia shortly before the battle of Actium (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Adoneus
source: Written Ἀδωνεύς. Strictly Adōneus. A surname of Bacchus, signifies the Ruler. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Adranus
source: Written Ἀδρανός. Strictly Adranos. A Sicilian divinity who was worshipped in all the island, but especially at Adranus, a town near Mount Aetna. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Agesander
source: Written Ἀγήσανδρος / Ἀγεσίλαος. Strictly Agēsandros. Or AGESILA'US, from ἄγειν and ἀνὴρ or λαός , a surname of Pluto or Hades, describing him as the god who carries away all men. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Agesias
source: Written Ἀγησίας. Strictly Agēsias. One of the lambidae, and an hereditary priest of Zeus at Olympia, gained the victory there in the mule race, and is celebrated on that accou (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Aglaus
source: Written Ἀγλαός. Strictly Aglaos. A poor citizen of Psophis in Arcadia, whom the Delphic oracle pronounced to be happier than Gyges, king of Lydia, on account of his contente (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Agnonides
source: Written Ἀγνωνίδης. Strictly Agnōnidēs. An Athenian demagogue and sycophant, a contemporary of Theophrastus and Phocion (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Algos
source: Written Ἄλγος. Is used by Hesiod (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Almops
source: Written Ἄλμωψ / Ἀλμωπία. Strictly Almōps. A giant, the son of Poseidon and Helle, from whom the district of Almopia and its inhabitants, the Almopes in Macedonia, were believed to ha (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Althepus
source: Written Ἄλθηπος. Strictly Althēpos. A son of Poseidon and Leis, a daughter of Orus, king of Troezen (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Alypus
source: Written Ἄλύπος. Strictly Alypos. A sculptor, a native of Sicyon (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Alyzeus
source: Written Ἀλυζεύς. A son of Icarius and brother of Penelope and Leucadius (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Amathes
source: Written Ἀμάθης / Ἀμαθούς. Strictly Amathēs. A son of Heracles, from whom the town of Amathus in Cyprus was believed to have derived its name (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ambryssus
source: Written Ἄμβρυσσος. Strictly Ambryssos. The mythical founder of the town of Ambryssus or Amphryssus in Phocis. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Amentes
source: Written Ἀμήντης. Strictly Amēntēs. An ancient Greek surgeon, mentioned by Galen as the inventor of some ingenious bandages. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ameristus
source: Written Ἀμέριστος. Strictly Ameristos. The brother of the poet Stesichorus, is mentioned by Proclus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Amiton
source: Written Ἀμίτων / Ἀμίτορες. Strictly Amitōn. Of Eleutherae in Crete, is said to have been the first person who sung to the lyre amatory poems (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Amorges
source: Written Ἀμόργης. Strictly Amorgēs. A king of the Sacae, according to Ctesias, whom Cyrus, king of Persia, conquered in battle, but afterwards released, when he himself was van (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Amphietes
source: Written Ἀμφιετής. Strictly Amphietēs. Or AMPHIE'TERUS, a surname of Dionysus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Amphis
source: Written Ἄμφις. An Athenian comic poet, of the middle comedy, contemporary with the philosopher Plato (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Amphissus
source: Written Ἄμφισσος. Strictly Amphissos. A son of Apollo and Dryope, is said to have been of extraordinary strength, and to have built the town of Oeta on the mountain of the same n (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ampycus
source: Written Ἄμπυκος. Strictly Ampykos. A son of Pelias, husband of Chloris, and father of the famous seer Mopsus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Amyclus
source: Written Ἄμυκλος / Ἀμύκλας. Strictly Amyklos. Or AMYCLAS (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Anaphas
source: Written Ἀναφᾶς. Was said to have been one of the seven who slew the Magi in B. C. 521 , and to have been lineally descended from Atossa, the sister of Camby (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Anchurus
source: Written Ἄγχουρος. Strictly Ankhouros. A son of the Phrygian king Midas, in whose reign the earth opened in the neighbourhood of the town of Celaenae in Phrygia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Anius
source: Written Ἄνιος. Strictly Anios. A son of Apollo by Creusa, or according to others by Rhoeo, the daughter of Staphylus, who when her pregnancy became known was exposed by he (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Anteias
source: Written Ἀντίας / Ἀντείας. Strictly Antias. Or ANTIAS, one of the three sons of Odysseus by Circe, from whom the town of Anteia in Italy was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Anthimus
source: Written Ἀνθίμος. Strictly Anthimos. Bishop of Trapezus in Pontus, was made patriarch of Constantinople by the influence of the empress Theodora, and about the same time was dra (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Anthippus
source: Written Ἄνθιππος / Ἀναξίππος. Strictly Anthippos. A Greek comic poet, a play of whose is cited by Athenaeus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Apemius
source: Written Ἀπήμιος. Strictly Apēmios. A surname of Zeus, under which he had an altar on mount Parnes in Attica, on which sacrifices were offered to him. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Aphepsion
source: Written Ἀφεψίων. Strictly Aphepsiōn. A son of Bathippus, who commenced operations against the law of Leptines respecting the abolition of exemptions from liturgies (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Apisaon
source: Written Ἀπισάων. Strictly Apisaōn. Two mythical personages of this name occur in the Iliad , 11.578, and 17.3481. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Apsyrtus
source: Written Ἄψυρτος. Strictly Apsyrtos. Or ABSYRTUS, one of the principal veterinary surgeons of whom any remains are still extant, was born, according to Suidas and Eudocia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Apteros
source: Written Ἄπτερος. "the wingless," a surname under which Nice had a sanctuary at Athens (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Aracus
source: Written Ἄρακος. Strictly Arakos. Ephor, B. C. 409 (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Araspes
source: Written Ἀράσπης. Strictly Araspēs. A Mede, and a friend of the elder Cyrus from his youth, contends with Cyrus that love has no power over him, but shortly afterwards refutes  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Arbius
source: Written Ἄρβιος. Strictly Arbios. A surname of Zeus, derived from mount Arbias in Crete, where he was worshipped. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ardalus
source: Written Ἄρδαλος. Strictly Ardalos. A son of Hephaestus, who was said to have invented the flute, and to have built a sanctuary of the Muses at Troezen, who derived from him th (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ardeas
source: Written Ἀρδέας. A son of Odysseus and Circe, the mythical founder of the town of Ardea in the country of the Rutuli. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Areilycus
source: Written Ἀρηίλυκος. Strictly Arēilykos. Two mythical personages of this name occur in the Iliad . (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Aresas
source: Written Ἀρέσας. Of Lucania, and probably of Croton, was at the head of the Pythagorean school, and the sixth in succession from Pythagoras (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Arethas
source: Written Ἀρέθας. Archbishop of Caesareia in Cappadocia at an uncertain time, appears to have succeeded ANDREAS. Works Commentary on the Apocalypse He wrote a (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Argalus
source: Written Ἄργαλος. Strictly Argalos. The eldest son of Amyclas, and his successor in the throne of Sparta. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ariaspes
source: Written Ἀριάσπης. Strictly Ariaspēs. Called by Justin Ariarates, one of the three legitimate sons of Artaxerxes Mnemon, was, after the death of his eldest brother Dareius, drive (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Arimazes
source: Written Ἀριμάζης / Ἀριομάζης. Strictly Arimazēs. Or ARIOMA'ZES, a chief who had possession, in B. C. 328 , of a very strong fortress in Sogdiana, usually called the Rock, which Droysen iden (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Arsites
source: Written Ἀρσίτης. Strictly Arsitēs. The satrap of the Hellespontine Phrygia when Alexander the Great invaded Asia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Artybius
source: Written Ἀρτύξιος. Strictly Artyxios. A Persian general in the reign of Dareius Hystaspis, who, after the Ionian revolt had broken out, sailed with a fleet to Cyprus to conquer t (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Asander
source: Written Ἄσανδρος. Strictly Asandros. A son of Philotas and brother of Parmenion (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ascalabus
source: Written Ἀσκάλαξος. Strictly Askalaxos. A son of Misme (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ascarus
source: Written Ἄσκαρος. Strictly Askaros. A Theban statuary, who made a statue of Zeus, dedicated by the Thessalians at Olympia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Athymbrus
source: Written Ἀθυμβρός / Ἀθύμβραδος. Strictly Athymbros. ATHYMBRADUS, and HYDRE'LUS, three brothers, who came from Lacedaemon, and founded cities in Lydia, which were called by their names (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Atrax
source: Written Ἄτραξ. A son of Peneius and Bura, from whom the town of Atrax in Hestiaeotis was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Atropates
source: Written Ἀτροπάτης. Strictly Atropatēs. Called Atrapes by Diodorus, a Persian satrap, apparently of Media, had the command of the Medes, together with the Cadusii, Albani, and Sace (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Aulonius
source: Written Αὐλώνιος. Strictly Aulōnios. A surname of Asclepius, derived from a temple he had in Aulon, a valley in Messenia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Auson
source: Written Αὔσων. Strictly Ausōn. A son of Odysseus either by Calypso or Circe. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Autaritus
source: Written Αὐτάριτος. Strictly Autaritos. The leader of the Gallic mercenaries in the Carthaginian army in Africa, took an active part in the rebellion against Carthage at the end of (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Autolaus
source: Written Αὐτόλαος. Strictly Autolaos. A son of Areas, who found and brought up the infant Asclepius when exposed in Thelpusa. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Autoleon
source: Written Αὐτολέων. Strictly Autoleōn. An ancient hero of Croton in southern Italy, concerning whom the following story is related :--It was customary with the Opuntian Locrians,  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Axieros
source: Written Ἀξίερος. A daughter of Cadmilus, and one of the three Samothracian Cabeiri (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Azanites
source: Written Ἀζανίτης. Strictly Azanitēs. A physician whose medical formulae appear to have enjoyed some celebrity, as they are quoted with approbation by Galen (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Azeus
source: Written Ἀζεύς. A son of Clymenus of Orchomenos, was a brother of Erginus, Stratius, Arrhon, and Pyleus, father of Actor and grandfather of Astyoche. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Babrius
source: Written Βάβριος / Βαβρίας. Strictly Babrios. Or BA'BRIAS, sometimes also called GA'BRIAS, who is not a different person from Babrius, as Bentley supposed, a Greek poet, who after the ex (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Barbillus
source: Written Βάρβιλλος. Strictly Barbillos. An astrologer at Rome in the reign of Vespasian. He was retained and consulted by the emperor, though all of his profession were forbidden t (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bardylis
source: Written Βάρδυλις / Βάρδυλλις. Or BARDYLLIS, the Illyrian chieftain, is said to have been originally a collier, --next, the leader of a band of freebooters, in which capac (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bargasus
source: Written Βάρψασος / Βάρψασα. Strictly Barpsasos. A son of Heracles and Barge, from whom the town of Bargasa in Caria derived its name (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bargylus
source: Written Βάργυλος / Βάρψυλα. Strictly Bargylos. A friend of Bellerophon, who was killed by Pegasus, and in commemoration of whom Bellerophon gave to a town in Caria the name of Bargyla. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Barzanes
source: Written Βαρζάνης. Strictly Barzanēs. One of the early kings of Armenia according to Diodorus, who makes him a tributary of the Assyrian Ninus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bassareus
source: Written Βασσαρεύς. A surname of Dionysus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Berosus
source: Written Βηρωσός / Βηρωσσρός. Strictly Bērōsos. A priest of Belus at Babylon, and an historian (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bestes
source: Written Βεστής. Strictly Bestēs. Perhaps Vestes, surnamed Conostaulus, a Greek interpreter of the Novells, filled the office of judex veli, and probably lived soon after the (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bisthanes
source: Written Βισθάνης. Strictly Bisthanēs. The son of Artaxerxes Ochus, met Alexander near Ecbatana, in B. C. 330 , and informed him of the flight of Dareius from that city. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bitys
source: Written Βίτυς. An Egyptian seer, who is said by Iamblichus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Blitor
source: Written Βλίτωρ. Strictly Blitōr. Satrap of Mesopotamia, was deprived of his satrapy by Antigonus in B. C. 316 , because he had allowed Seleucus to escape from Babylon to Egy (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bodon
source: Written Βώδων / Βωδώνη. Strictly Bōdōn. An ancient hero, from whom the Thessalian town of Bodone derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bogud
source: Written Βογούας. Strictly Bogouas. Was king of Mauretania Tingitana, in which title he was confirmed by Julius Caesar, B. C. 49 , as a reward for his adherence to him in oppos (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bomilcar
source: Written Βομίλκας / Βοαμίλκας. Strictly Bomilkas. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bormus
source: Written Βῶρμος / Βῶριμος. Strictly Bōrmos. A son of Upius, a Mariandynian,. was a youth distinguished for his extraordinary beauty (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bostar
source: Written Βώστωρ. Strictly Bōstōr. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Branchus
source: Written Βράγχος. Strictly Brankhos. A son of Apollo or Smicrus of Delphi (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Brangas
source: Written Βράγγας. A son of the Thracian king Strymon, and brother of Rhessus and Olynthus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Brentus
source: Written Βρέντος / Βρεντήσιον. Strictly Brentos. A son of Heracles, who was regarded as the founder of the town of Brentesium or Brundusium, on the Adriatic. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Brettus
source: Written Βρέττος. Strictly Brettos. A son of Heracles, from whom the Tyrrhenian town of Brettus and the country of Brettia derived their names. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Broteas
source: Written Βροτέας. A boil of Vulcan and Minerva, who burnt himself that he might not be taunted with his ugliness. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Brusus
source: Written Βροῦσος / Βροῦσις. Strictly Brousos. A son of Emathius, from whom Brusis, a portion of Macedonia, was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Brutius
source: Written Βρούτιος. Strictly Broutios. An historian and chronographer, is called by the writer of the Alexandrian chronicle (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Buphagus
source: Written Βούφαγος. Strictly Bouphagos. A son of Iapetus and Thornaxe, an Arcadian hero and husband of Promne (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Buraicus
source: Written Βουραϊκός. Strictly Bouraikos. A surname of Heracles, derived from the Achaean town of Bura, near which he had a statue on the river Buraicus, and an oracle in a cave (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Burichus
source: Written Βούριχος. Strictly Bourikhos. One of the commanders of Demetrius Poliorcetes in the sea-fight off Cyprus, B. C. 306 , was one of the flatterers of the king, to whom the A (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Butas
source: Written Βούρτας. Strictly Bourtas. A Greek poet of uncertain age, wrote in elegiac verse an account of early Roman history, from which Plutarch quotes the fabulous origin of t (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Byzas
source: Written Βύζας. A son of Poseidon and Ceroessa, the daughter of Zeus and Io (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cabarnus
source: Written Κάβαρνος. Strictly Kabarnos. A mythical personage of the island of Paros, who revealed to Demeter the fact of her daughter having been carried off, and from whom the isl (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Calanus
source: Written Κάλανος. Strictly Kalanos. One of the so-called gymnosophists of India, who followed the Macedonian army from Taxila at the desire of Alexander the Great; but when he  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Callines
source: Written Καλλίνης. Strictly Kallinēs. A veteran officer in the royal companion-cavalry of Alexander the Great, took an active part in the reconciliation between him and his army  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cambaules
source: Written Καμβαύλης. Strictly Kambaulēs. The leader of a horde of Gauls before they invaded Greece in B. C. 279 . The barbarians were at first few in number, but when they reached T (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Candybus
source: Written Κάνδυβος. Strictly Kandybos. A son of Deucalion, from whom Candyba, a town in Lycia, was believed to have received its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Carthalo
source: Written Καρθάλων. Strictly Karthalōn. A commander of the Carthaginian fleet in the first Punic war, who was sent by his colleague Adherbal, in B. C. 249 , to burn the Roman fleet (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Castorion
source: Written Καστορίων. Strictly Kastoriōn. Of Soli, is mentioned by Athenaeus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Coluthus
source: Written Κόλουθος. Strictly Kolouthos. One of the late Greek epic poets, was a native of Lycopolis in Upper Egypt, and flourished under the emperor Anastasius, at the beginning of (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Conisalus
source: Written Κονίδαλος. Strictly Konidalos. A daemon, who together with Orthanes and Tychon appeared in the train of Priapus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Conius
source: Written Κόνιος. Strictly Konios. The god who excites or makes dust, a surname of Zeus, who had an uncovered temple under this name in the arx of Megara. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Corniades
source: Written Κορνιάδης. Strictly Korniadēs. An intimate friend of Epicurus, is spoken of by Cicero (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cresius
source: Written Κρήσιος. Strictly Krēsios. A surname of Dionysus at Argos, where he had a temple in which Ariadne was said to be buried. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Creteus
source: Written Κρητεύς. Strictly Krēteus. Or CATREUS, a son of Minos by Pasiphae or Crete, and king of Crete (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cromus
source: Written Κρῶμος. Strictly Krōmos. A son of Poseidon, from whom Cromyon in the territory of Corinth was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Damogeron
source: Written Δαμογέρων. Strictly Damogerōn. A Greek writer on agriculture, concerning whom nothing at all is known, although fifteen extracts from his work are still extant in the Geop (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Daunus
source: Written Δαῦνος / Δαύνιος. Strictly Daunos. A son of Lycaon in Arcadia, and brother of Iapyx and Peucetius (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Dectades
source: Written Δεκτάδης. Strictly Dektadēs. Is mentioned by Parthenius (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Dection
source: Written Δεκτίων. Strictly Dektiōn. A Greek grammarian, who wrote a commentary on Lycophron's Cassandra, which is referred to in the Etymologicum Magnum (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Democoon
source: Written Δεμοκόων. Strictly Demokoōn. A natural son of Priam, who came from Abydos to assist his father against the Greeks, but was slain by Odysseus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Diocorus
source: Written Διόκορος / Διόσκορος. Strictly Diokoros. Or DIO'SCORUS, a commentator on the orations of Demosthenes. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Dolabella
source: Written Δολαβέλλας. Strictly Dolabellas. Sometimes written Dolobella, the name of a family of the patrician Cornelia gens. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Domatites
source: Written Δοματίτης. Strictly Domatitēs. That is, the domestic, a surname of Poseidon, at Sparta, which is, perhaps, synonymous with ἐπιχώριος . (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Doxipater
source: Written Δοξίπατρος. Strictly Doxipatros. Or DOXO'PA TER, JOANNES, a Greek grammarian or rhetorician (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Dysaules
source: Written Δυσαύλης. Strictly Dysaulēs. The father of Triptolemus and Eubuleus, and a brother of Celeus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ebion
source: Written Ἐβίων. Strictly Ebiōn. The real or supposed founder of the sect of Christians called Ebionites, by which name, at least after the time of Irenaeus, were designated (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ecdicus
source: Written Ἔκδικος. Strictly Ekdikos. A Lacedaemonian, was sent out with eight ships, in B. C. 391 , to put down the democratic party in Rhodes (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Echemon
source: Written Ἐχέμων. Strictly Ekhemōn. A son of Priam, who was killed, with his brother Chromius, by Diomedes. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Edecon
source: Written Ἐδεκών. Strictly Edekōn. An Iberian chief, called Edesco by Livy (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Elaphus
source: Written Ἔλαφος. Strictly Elaphos. The fifteenth in descent from Aesculapius, the son of Chrysus and the farther of Hippolochus II., who lived probably in the island of Cos in (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Eleuther
source: Written Ἐλευθήρ / Ἐλευθεραί. Strictly Eleuthēr. A son of Apollo and Aethusa, the daughter of Poseidon, was regarded as the founder of Eleutherae in Boeotia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Emathus
source: Written Ἤμαθος. Strictly Ēmathos. A son of Macedon and brother of Pierus, from whom Emathia, that is Macedonia, was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Emilus
source: Written Ἔμιλος. Strictly Emilos. Of Aegina, made the gold and ivory statues of the Hours sitting on thrones in the temple of Hera at Olympia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Empodus
source: Written Ἔμποδος. Strictly Empodos. An otherwise unknown writer, whose ἀπομνημονεύματα are mentioned by Athenaeus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Enalus
source: Written Ἔναλος. Strictly Enalos. The Penthelides, the first settlers in Lesbos, had received an oracle from Amphitrite commanding them to sacrifice a bull to Poseidon and a  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Endius
source: Written Ἔνδιος. Strictly Endios. Of Sparta, son of Alcibiades, member of a family whose connexion with that of the Athenian Alcibiades had ina previous generation introduced (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Enorches
source: Written Ἐνόρχης. Strictly Enorkhēs. A son of Thyestes by his sister Daeta, was born out of an egg, and built a temple to Dionysus, who was hence called Dionysus Enorches, thoug (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Epicurius
source: Written Ἐπικούριος. Strictly Epikourios. The helper, a surname of Apollo, under which he was worshipped at Bassae in Arcadia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Epidotes
source: Written Ἐπιδώτης. Strictly Epidōtēs. A divinity who was worshipped at Lacedaemon, and averted the anger of Zeus Hicesius for the crime committed by Pausanias. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Eresus
source: Written Ἔρεσος. Strictly Eresos. A son of Macar, from whom the town of Eresus in Lesbos derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Eribotes
source: Written Ἐριβώτης. Strictly Eribōtēs. The son of Teleon, was one of the Argonauts, and appears to have acted as surgeon, as he is represented as attending on Oileus when he was w (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Eriphus
source: Written Ἔριφος. Strictly Eriphos. An Athenian comic poet of the middle comedy (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Eriunius
source: Written Ἐριούνιος. Strictly Eriounios. Or ERINNES, the giver of good fortune, occurs as a surname of Hermes, but is also used as a proper name instead of Hermes. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Erymas
source: Written Ἐρύμας. The name of three different Trojans. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Eubotas
source: Written Εὐβώτας / Εὔβατος. Strictly Eubōtas. A Cyrenaean, who gained a victory in the foot-race in Ol (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Eubuleus
source: Written Εὐβουλεύς. Strictly Eubouleus. According to an Argive tradition, a son of Trochilus by an Eleusinian woman, and brother of Triptolemus; whereas, according to the Orphici,  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Eugamon
source: Written Εὐγάηων. Strictly Eugaēōn. One of the Cyclic poets (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Eugeon
source: Written Εὐγέων / Εὐγαίων. Strictly Eugeōn. Of Samos, one of the earliest Greek historians mentioned by Dionysius of Halicarnassus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Europs
source: Written Εὔρωψ. Strictly Eurōps. The name of two mythical personages, the one a son of Aegialeus and king of Sicyon, and the other a son of Phoroneus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Europus
source: Written Εὔρωπός. Strictly Eurōpos. A son of Macedon and Oreithyia, the daughter of Cecrops, from whom the town of Europus in Macedonia was believed to have received its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Eurypon
source: Written Εὐρυπῶν / Εὐρυτίων. Strictly Eurypōn. Grandson of Procles, was the third king of that house at Sparta, and thenceforward gave it the name of Eurypontidae (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Evanemus
source: Written Εὐάνεμος. Strictly Euanemos. The giver of favourable wind, was a surname of Zeus, under which the god had a sanctuary at Sparta. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ezekielus
source: Written Ἐζεκιῆλος. Strictly Ezekiēlos. Works ἐξαγωγή, the author of a work in Greek entitled ἐξαγωγή , which is usually called a tragedy, but which seems rather to have been a met (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Galaton
source: Written Γαλάτων. Strictly Galatōn. A Greek painter, whose picture, representing Homer vomiting, and other poets gathering up what fell from him, is mentioned by Aelian (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Galaxius
source: Written Γαλάξιος. Strictly Galaxios. A surname of Apollo in Boeotia, derived from the stream Galaxius. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Gaos
source: Written Γαώς. Strictly Gaōs. The commander of the Persian fleet, in the great expedition sent by Artaxerxes against Evagoras in Cyprus, B. C. 386 . In this situation he  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Gauradas
source: Written Γαυράδας. The author of an epigram in the Greek Anthology, in the Doric dialect, of that fanciful kind in which an echo is made to repeat the last wor (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Gelimer
source: Written Γελίμερ. Last king of the Vandals, son of Gelaris, grandson of Genzo, and great-grandson of Genseric, who, bv the imprisonment and subsequent murder  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Gentius
source: Written Γέντιος / Γενθιος. Strictly Gentios. Son of Pleuratus, a king of the Illyrians. contemporary with Perseus, the last king of Macedonia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Gisco
source: Written Γίσκων. Strictly Giskōn. Or GISGO (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Golgus
source: Written Γόλγος. Strictly Golgos. A son of Adonis and Aphrodite, from whom the town of Golgi, in Cyprus, was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Gordys
source: Written Γόρδυς / Γορδίειον. A son of Triptolemus, who assisted in searching after Io, and then settled in Phrygia, where the district of Gordyaea received its name from (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Gortys
source: Written Γόρτυς. A son of Stymphelus, and founder of the Arcadian town of Gortys. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Gundamund
source: Written Γουνδαμοῦνδος. Strictly Goundamoundos. Son of Genzo, and grandson of Genseric, succeeded his uncle Hunneric as king of the Vandals, and reigned from A. D. 484 to 496. He persecute (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hagnon
source: Written Ἅγνων. Strictly Hagnōn. Son of Nicias. was the Athenian founder of Amphipolis, on the Strymon (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Haliartus
source: Written Ἁλίαρτυς. Strictly Haliartys. A son of Thersander, and grandson of Sisyphus, was believed to have founded the town of lHaliartus in Boeotia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Halmus
source: Written Ἅλμος. Strictly Halmos. A son of Sisyphus, and father of Chryse and Chrysogeneia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hamilcar
source: Written Ἁμίλκας / Ἀμίλχαρ. Strictly Hamilkas. The two last syllables of this name are considered by (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Harpocras
source: Written Ἁρπόκρας. Strictly Harpokras. An iatralipta, who attended the younger Pliny, with great care and assiduity, about the beginning of the second century after Christ (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hedylus
source: Written Ἥδυλος. Strictly Hēdylos. The son of Melicertus, was a native of Samos or of Athens, and an epigrammatic poet (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hegeleos
source: Written Ἡγέλεως. Strictly Hēgeleōs. A son of Tyrsenus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hegetor
source: Written Ἡγήτωρ. Strictly Hēgētōr. A surgeon, who probably lived at Alexandria at the end of the second or the beginning of the first century B. C., as he is apparently mentio (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Helianax
source: Written Ἡλιάναξ. Strictly Hēlianax. Brother of Stesichorus, who, according to Suidas, was a lawgiver, probably in one of the states of Sicily (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Helixus
source: Written Ἕλιξος. Strictly Helixos. Of Megara, with a portion of the Lacedaemonian squadron, which, on its way to the Hellespont, under Clearchus, was dispersed by a storm, mad (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Helladius
source: Written Ἑλλάδιος. Strictly Helladios. Of Alexandria, a grammarian in the time of Theodosius the younger (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Helorus
source: Written Ἑλωρός. Strictly Helōros. A son of the Scythian Istrus, and brother of Actaeus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hemitheon
source: Written Ἡμιθέων. Strictly Hēmitheōn. A Sybarite of the vilest character, and the author of an obscene work (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Heniochus
source: Written Ἡνίοχος. Strictly Hēniokhos. An Athenian comic poet of the middle comedy, whose plays, as mentioned by Suidas, were: Τροχίλος, Ἐπίκληρος, Γοργόνες, Πολυπράγμων, Θωρύκιον (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Heracon
source: Written Ἡράκων. Strictly Hērakōn. An officer in the service of Alexander , who, together with Cleander and Sitalces, succeeded to the command of the army in Media, which had  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Heragoras
source: Written Ἡραγόρας. Strictly Hēragoras. A Greek historian of uncertain date (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Heras
source: Written Ἥρας. Strictly Hēras. A physician of Cappadocia, who lived after Heracleides of Tarentum (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Herculius
source: Written Ἑρκούλιος. Strictly Herkoulios. Praefectus praetorio Illyrici, A. D. 408 - 412 , is probably the Herculius to whom one of the letters of Chrysostom is addressed (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hereas
source: Written Ἡρέας. Strictly Hēreas. An historical writer, a native of Megara, quoted by Plutarch (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Herminus
source: Written Ἑρμῖνος. Strictly Herminos. A Peripatetic philosopher, a contemporary of Demonax (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hermocles
source: Written Ἑρμοκλῆς. Strictly Hermoklēs. Of Rhodes, a statuary, who made the bronze statue of Combabus in the temple of Hera at Hierapolis in Syria (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Herodorus
source: Written Ἡρόδωρος. Strictly Hērodōros. A native of Heracleia, in Pontus, who appears to have lived about the time of Hecataeus of Miletus and Pherecydes, in the latter part of the (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hiarbas
source: Written Ἱάρβας. A king of the Numidians, who supported Domitius Ahenobarbus and the remains of the Marian party in Africa (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hierius
source: Written Ἱέριος. Strictly Hierios. A rhetorician of Athens, who is mentioned by St (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hilarius
source: Written Ἱλάριος. Strictly Hilarios. A Phrygian, an interpreter of oracles, implicated in the proceedings of Theodorus, who attempted to discover by magic who should succeed the (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hilderic
source: Written Ἱλδέριχος. Strictly Hilderikhos. King of the Vandals, son of Hunncric, and grandson of Hilderic, successor of Trasamund, reigned A. D. 523 - 530 . He was of a gentle disposi (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Himerius
source: Written Ἱμέριος. Strictly Himerios. A celebrated Greek sophist of Prusa in Bithynia, where his father Ameinias distinguished himself as a rhetorician. According to the most cor (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Himilco
source: Written Ἱμίλκων / Ἱμίλκας. Strictly Himilkōn. Considerable variations are found in the MSS. in the mode of writing this name, which is frequently confounded with Hamilcar, and written Ἀμ (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hippasius
source: Written Ἱππάσιος. Strictly Hippasios. A veterinary surgeon, who may perhaps have lived in the fourth or fifth century after Christ (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hippeus
source: Written Ἱππεύς. A painter, whose picture at Athens of the marriage of Peirithoüs is mentioned by Polemon. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hippitas
source: Written Ἱππίτας / Ἱππότας. Or HI'PPOTAS, one of the friends of Cleomenes III., king of Sparta, who accompanied him in his flight and exile in Egypt (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hippocles
source: Written Ἱπποκλῆς. Strictly Hippoklēs. Son of Menippus took post off Leucas, with 27 Athenian galleys, in the year following the Sicilian defeat, B. C. 412 , to watch for the retu (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hipponax
source: Written Ἱππῶναξ. Strictly Hippōnax. Of Ephesus, the son of Pytheus and Protis, was, after Archilochus and Simonides, the third of the classical Iambic poets of Greece. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hippys
source: Written Ἵππυς / Ἵπυς. Of Rhegium, a Greek historian, who lived in the time of the Persian wars, and wrote a work on Sicily in five books, which was epitomised by  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Holmus
source: Written Ὅλμος. Strictly Holmos. A son of Sisyphus, and father of Minyas (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Horapollo
source: Written Ὡραπόλλων. Strictly Hōrapollōn. Was, according to Suidas, a very distinguished Greek grammarian of Phaenebythis in Egypt, who first taught at Alexandria, and afterwards at  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hosius
source: Written Ὅσιος. Strictly Hosios. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hybreas
source: Written Ὑβρέας. Of Mylasa in Caria, was, according to Strabo, the greatest orator of his time (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hybrias
source: Written Ὑβρίας. Of Crete, a lyric poet, the author of a highly esteemed scholion which is preserved by Athenaeus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hylatus
source: Written Ὕλατος. Strictly Hylatos. A surname of Apollo derived from the town of Hyle in Crete, which was sacred to him. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hymeas
source: Written Ὑμέης. Strictly Hymeēs. A son-in-law of Dareius Hystaspis, acted as a general of his against the revolted Ionians, and was one of those who defeated the rebels near (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hypatus
source: Written Ὕπατος. Strictly Hypatos. The most high, occurs not only as an epithet of Zeus in poetry (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hyperes
source: Written Ὑπέρης. Strictly Hyperēs. A son of Poseidon and Alcyone, and king of Troezene, from whom the town of Hypereia derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hyperides
source: Written Ὑπερείδης / Ὑπερίδης. Strictly Hypereidēs. A celebrated Attic orator, was the son of Glaucippus, and belonged to the Attic demus of Collytus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hypsenor
source: Written Ὑψήνωρ. Strictly Hypsēnōr. The name of two mythical personages, one a son of the Trojan priest Dolopion, who was killed by Eurypylus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hypseus
source: Written Ὑψεύς. A son of Peneius, and the Naiad Creusa, or Phillyra, the daughter of Asopus, was king of the Lapithae, and married to Chlidanope, by whom he (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hypsicles
source: Written Ὑψικλῆς. Strictly Hypsiklēs. Was of Alexandria, or, as the Arabic writers say, of Ascalon (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hypsus
source: Written Ὕψος. Strictly Hypsos. A son of Lycaon. believed to have been the founder of Hypsus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hysmon
source: Written Ὕσμων. Strictly Hysmōn. An Eleian athlete, who began when a boy to practise the pentathlon as a cure for rheumatism, and who was victorious in that kind of contest, (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ialemus
source: Written Ἰάλεμος. Strictly Ialemos. A similar personification to that of Linus, and hence alo called a son of Apollo and Calliope, and the inventor of the song Ialemus, which w (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Iambulus
source: Written Ἰάμβουλος. Strictly Iamboulos. A Greek author, who is known for having written a work on the strange forms and figures of the inhabitants of India. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Iamus
source: Written Ἴαμος. Strictly Iamos. A son of Apollo and Evadne, was initiated in the art of prophecy by his father, and was regarded as the ancestor of the famous family of see (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ianiscus
source: Written Ἰάνισκος. Strictly Ianiskos. The name of two mythical personages. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Iasus
source: Written Ἴασος. Strictly Iasos. The name of a considerable number of mythical personages, which is sometimes written Iasius, and is etymologically the same as Iason and Ias (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Iccus
source: Written Ἴκκος. Strictly Ikkos. Of Tarentum, a distinguished athlete and teacher of gymnastics (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Imbramus
source: Written Ἴμβραμος. Strictly Imbramos. A surname of Hermes (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Imbrasus
source: Written Ἴμβρασος. Strictly Imbrasos. Is, according to Eustathius (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Immaradus
source: Written Ἰμμάραδος. Strictly Immarados. A son of Eumolpus, and commander of the Eleusinians, slain by Erectheus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Indibilis
source: Written Ἰνδίβιλις. A king or chief of the Spanish tribe of the Ilergetes, who plays an important part in the war between the Romans and Carthaginians in Spain  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Iocastus
source: Written Ἰόκαστος. Strictly Iokastos. A son of Aeolis, king on the coast of Italy in the district of Rhegium. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ionides
source: Written Ἰωνίδες / Ἰωνιάδες. Strictly Iōnides. A name borne by four nymphs believed to possess healing powers (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Iops
source: Written Ἴοψ. A hero who had a sanctuary at Sparta. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ioxus
source: Written Ἴοξος. Strictly Ioxos. A son of Melanippus, and grandson of Theseus and Perigune, is said to have led a colony into Caria, in conjunction with Ornytus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ischander
source: Written Ἴσχανδρος. Strictly Iskhandros. An obscure Athenian tragic poet, in whose plays Aeschines is said to have acted. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ischenus
source: Written Ἴσχενος. Strictly Iskhenos. Also called Taraxippus, from the hores becoming shy on his tomb, is said to have allowed himself to be sacrificed for the purpose of avertin (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Isodetes
source: Written Ἰσοδέτης. Strictly Isodetēs. From δέω , the god who binds all equally, is used as a surname of Pluto, to express his impartiality, and of Apollo. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ithomatas
source: Written Ἰθώματας. Strictly Ithōmatas. A surname of Zeus derived from the Messenian hill of Ithome, where the god had a sanctuary, and where an annual festival, the Ithomaea, was  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ixius
source: Written Ἴξιος / Ἴξιαι. Strictly Ixios. A surname of Apollo, derived from a district of the island of Rhodes which was called Ixiae or Ixia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Izates
source: Written Ἰζάτης. Strictly Izatēs. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Khosru
source: Written Χοσρόης. Strictly Khosroēs. KHOSRU , or KHOSREW I., called CHOSROES I. by the Greeks, surnamed ANUSHIRWAN, or "the generous mind," one of the greatest monarchs of Persi (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Kobad
source: Written Κοβάδης. Strictly Kobadēs. KOBAD , or COBADES, reigned from A. D. 488 to 498, and again from 501 or 502 till 531. The years from 498 till 502 were filled up by the sho (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ladogenes
source: Written Λαδωγενής / Λαδωνίς. Strictly Ladōgenēs. Or LADO'NIS, a name by which the poets sometimes designated Daphne, the daughter of Ladon. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lapersius
source: Written Λαπέρσιος. Strictly Lapersios. A surname of Zeus, derived from the Attic demus of Lapersae. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lecheates
source: Written Λεχεάτης. Strictly Lekheatēs. I. e. the protector of childbed, a surname of Zeus, who, as the father of Athena, was worshipped under this name at Aliphera. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Leches
source: Written Λέχης. Strictly Lekhēs. A son of Poseidon and Peirene, and brother of Cenchrias. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lentulus
source: Written Λέντλος. Strictly Lentlos. The name of one of the haughtiest patrician families of the Cornelian Gens; so that Cicero coins the words Appietas and Lentulitas to expres (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Letreus
source: Written Λετρεύς. A son of Pelops, and the reputed founder of Letrini, on the western coast of Peloponnesus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Litorius
source: Written Λιτώριος. Strictly Litōrios. A veterinary surgeon, a native of Beneventum in Samnium, who may, perhaps, have lived in the fourth or fifth century after Christ (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lycastus
source: Written Λύκαστος. Strictly Lykastos. A son of Minos and Itone, was king of Crete and husband of Ida, the daughter of Corybas (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lydiades
