source: Written Λυδιάδης / Λυσιάδης. Strictly Lydiadēs. Λυδιάδης . There is, however, considerable doubt whether this or Λυσιάδης is the more correct forms of the name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lyncus
source: Written Λύγκος. Strictly Lynkos. A king of Scythia, or, according to others, of Sicily, wanted to murder Triptolemus, who came to him with the gifts of Ceres, in order to se (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lyrcus
source: Written Λύρκος. Strictly Lyrkos. The name of two mythical personages. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lysius
source: Written Λύσιος. Strictly Lysios. I. e. the Deliverer, a surname of Dionysus, under which he was worshipped at Corinth, where there was a carved image of the god, the whole f (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lyterius
source: Written Λυτήριος. Strictly Lytērios. I. e. the Deliverer, a surname of Pan, under which he had a sanctuary at Troezene, because he was believed during a plague to have revealed  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lytierses
source: Written Λυτιέρσης. Strictly Lytiersēs. Another form of Lityerses. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Madates
source: Written Μαδέτας. Strictly Madetas. Called by Diodorus MA'DETAS,, a general of Dareius, who defended a strong mountain--fortress of the Uxii against Alexander the Great, when t (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Magadates
source: Written Μαγαδάτης. Strictly Magadatēs. General of Tigranes, king of Armenia, was entrusted by him with the government of Syria, when it had been conquered from Antiochus X. in B.  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Maharbal
source: Written Μαάρβας. Strictly Maarbas. Son of Himilco, and one of the most distinguished Carthaginian officers in the Second Punic War (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Maleates
source: Written Μαλεάτης. Strictly Maleatēs. A surname of Apollo, derived from cape Malea, in the south of Laconia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Maleus
source: Written Μάλεος. Strictly Maleos. A son of Heracles by Omphale, is said to have been the inventor of the trumpet. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mamertus
source: Written Μάμερτος. Strictly Mamertos. An ancient surname of Ares, which must have arisen after the identification of the Italian Mamers with the Greek Ares. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Manetho
source: Written Μανεθώς / Μανεθών. Strictly Manethōs. Μανεθώς * His original Egyptian name was undoubtedly Manethōth, that is, Ma-ϟ-thôith, or the one given by Thoth, which would be expressed by (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mannus
source: Written Μάννος. Strictly Mannos. A king of some part of Arabia bordering upon Mesopotamia, who submitted to Trajan on his expedition against the Parthians. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Margites
source: Written Μαργίτης. Strictly Margitēs. The hero of a comic epic poem, which most of the ancients regarded as a work of Homer (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Marmax
source: Written Μάρμαξ. One of the suitors of Hippodameia, who was slain by Oenomaus, and was buried with his two horses, Parthenia and Eripha. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Masinissa
source: Written Μασσανάσσης. Strictly Massanassēs. King of the Numidians, celebrated for the conspicuous part he bore in the wars between the Romans and Carthaginians (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mastor
source: Written Μάστωρ. Strictly Mastōr. Two mythical personages, one the father of Lycophron in Cythera (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mechaneus
source: Written Μηχανεύς. Strictly Mēkhaneus. Skilled in inventing, was a surname of Zeus at Argos (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Medeon
source: Written Μηδεών. Strictly Mēdeōn. A son of Pylades and Electra, from whom the town of Medeon in Phocis was believed to have received its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Megarus
source: Written Μέγαρος. Strictly Megaros. A son of Zeus, by a Sithnian or Megarian nymph (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Meliteus
source: Written Μελιτεύς. A son of Zeus by an Othreian nymph (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Melitodes
source: Written Μελιτώδης. Strictly Melitōdēs. I. e. sweet as honey, occurs as a Euphemistic surname of Persephone. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Melus
source: Written Μῆλος. Strictly Mēlos. A son of Manto, from whom the sanctuary of Apollo Malloeis in Lesbos was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mendes
source: Written Μένδης. Strictly Mendēs. An Egyptian divinity, worshipped in the town of Mendes (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Meryllus
source: Written Μέρυλλος. Strictly Meryllos. A Greek writer, who wrote a work on Boeotia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Messalla
source: Written Μεσσάλας. Strictly Messalas. A cognomen of the Gens Valeria at Rome, was originally assumed by M. Valerius Maximus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Messapeus
source: Written Μεσσαπεύς. A surname of Zeus, under which he had a sanctuary between Amyclae and mount Taygetus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Messapus
source: Written Μέσσαπος. Strictly Messapos. A Boeotian, from whom Mount Messapion, on the coast of Boeotia, and Messapia, in southern Italy, were believed to have derived their names. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Metabus
source: Written Μέταβος. Strictly Metabos. A son of Sisyphus, from whom the town of Metapontum, in Southern Italy, was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Methapus
source: Written Μέθαπος. Strictly Methapos. An Athenian who is said to have introduced at Thebes the worship of the Cabeiri (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Methodius
source: Written Μεθόδιος. Strictly Methodios. Surnamed the APOSTLE of Bohemia, enjoys great reputation in the history of the church as well as of the fine arts (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mideatis
source: Written Μιδεᾶτις. A surname of Alcmene. derived from the town of Midea in Argolis, where her father Electryon ruled as king. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mimallon
source: Written Μιμαλλών / Μιμαλών. Strictly Mimallōn. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mithrenes
source: Written Μιθρήνης / Μιθρίνης. Strictly Mithrēnēs. Or MITHRI'NES, commander of the Persian force which garrisoned the citadel of Sardes (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mochus
source: Written Μωχός. Strictly Mōkhos. A native of Phoenicia, the author of a work on Phoenician history quoted by Athenaeus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Monobazus
source: Written Μονόβαζος. Strictly Monobazos. Was king or tetrarch of Adiabene in A. D. 63 , when Tigranes, king of Armenia, invaded his kingdom (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Morzes
source: Written Μορζίας. Strictly Morzias. Or, according to Polybius, MO'RZIAS, a king of Paphlagonia, who fought against the Romans in the Gallo-Graecian war, B. C. 189 . Morzes had  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mutines
source: Written Μουτίνας. Strictly Moutinas. An African by birth, belonging to the halfcaste race called the Lybio-Phoenicians (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mynes
source: Written Μύνης. Strictly Mynēs. A son of Evenus of Lyrnesus, and husband of Briseis, was slain by Achilles. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Myniscus
source: Written Μυνίσκος. Strictly Myniskos. A tragic actor, a native of Chalcis, who was attacked by Plato in his comedy called Σύρφαξ , on account of his gluttony (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Naravas
source: Written Ναραύας. Strictly Narauas. A Numidian chief, who bears a conspicuous part in the war of the Carthaginians against their revolted mercenaries and African subjects (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Nemeius
source: Written Νεμεῖος. Strictly Nemeios. The Nemeian, a surname of Zeus, under which he had a sanctuary at Argos, with a bronze statue, the work of Lysippus, and where games were ce (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Niphates
source: Written Νιφάτης. Strictly Niphatēs. One of the Persian generals in the battle of the Granicus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Nonnosus
source: Written Νόννοσος. Strictly Nonnosos. Was sent by the emperor Justinian I. on an embassy to the Aethiopians, Ameritae, Saracens, and other Eastern nations (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Nypsius
source: Written Νύψιος. Strictly Nypsios. A native of Neapolis, and a brave and skilful officer, who was sent by the younger Dionysius to the relief of the citadel at Syracuse, which (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Oaxes
source: Written Ὄαξος. Strictly Oaxos. Or OAXUS, the mythical founder of the town of Oaxus in Crete, is said by some to have been a son of Acacallis, the daughter of Minos (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Obrimus
source: Written Ὄβριμος. Strictly Obrimos. Or O'MBRIMUS, a Greek rhetorician, probably of Asia, but of uncertain date, two of whose orations are quoted by Stobaeus, namely , Πρωτογόνο (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ochimus
source: Written Ὄχιμος. Strictly Okhimos. A Rhodian king, a son of Helios and Rhodos (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ogygus
source: Written Ὠγύγης. Strictly Ōgygēs. Or OGY'GES, is sometimes called a Boeotian autochthon, and sometimes a son of Boeotus, and king of the Hectenes, and the first ruler of the  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Olthacus
source: Written Ὀλθακός. Strictly Olthakos. A chief of the Scythian tribe of the Dandarians, who served in the arny of Mithridates the Great, and enjoyed a high place in the favour of  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Olymnius
source: Written Ὀλύμνιος. Strictly Olymnios. A physician of Alexandria, whose date is unknown, the author of a work on Critical Days, to be found in MS. in the king's library at Paris. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Omadius
source: Written Ὠμάδιος. Strictly Ōmadios. That is, the flesh-eater, a surname of Dionysus, to whom human sacrifices were offered in Chios and Tenedos. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ombrius
source: Written Ὄμβριος. Strictly Ombrios. I. e. the rain-giver, a surname of Zeus, under which he had an altar on Mount Hymettus in Attica. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Onasus
source: Written Ὄνασος. Strictly Onasos. The author of a work on the Amazons, entitled Ἀμαζονίς or Ἀμαζονικά , which was supposed by Heyne (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Oncus
source: Written Ὄγκος. Strictly Onkos. A son of Apollo, and founder of Onceium in Arcadia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Oneiros
source: Written Ὄνειρος. A personification of dream, and in the plural of dreams (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Origenes
source: Written Ὠριγένης. Strictly Ōrigenēs. One of the most eminent of the early Christian writers, not only for his intellectual powers and attainments, but also for the influence exe (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Orneus
source: Written Ὀρνεύς. A son of Erechtheus, father of Peteus, and grandfather of Menestheus; from him the town of Orneae was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ornytion
source: Written Ὀρνυτίων. Strictly Ornytiōn. A Corinthian, was the son of Sisyphus, and the father of Phocus and Thoas. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Orodes
source: Written Ὀρώδης. Strictly Orōdēs. A name common to many Eastern monarchs, of whom the Parthian kings were the most celebrated (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ortiagon
source: Written Ὀρτιάγων. Strictly Ortiagōn. One of the three princes of Galatia, when that country was invaded by the Romans under Cn (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Orxines
source: Written Ὀρξίνης. Strictly Orxinēs. A noble and wealthy Persian, who traced his descent from Cyrus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Oxycanus
source: Written Ὀξυκανός. Strictly Oxykanos. Or PORTICANUS, as he is called by Q. Curtius, an Indian prince, whose territories lay to the west of those of Musicanus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Oxyntas
source: Written Ὀξύντας. Son of Jugurtha, was led captive, together with his father, before the triumphal car of Marius; but his life was spared, and he was placed i (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pachomius
source: Written Παχώμιος / Παχούμιος. Strictly Pakhōmios. As Socrates and Palladius write the name, or PACHU'MIUS, according to the author of the Vita Pachumii, an Egyptian ascetic of the fourth cen (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pacorus
source: Written Πάκορος. Strictly Pakoros. A conmmon Parthian name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Palicus
source: Written Παλικός / Παλικοί. Strictly Palikos. Commonly found in the plural Palici, Παλικοί , were Sicilian daemons, twin sons of Zeus and the nymph Thaleia, the daughter of Hephaestus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Palladas
source: Written Παλλάδας. The author of a large number of epigrams in the Greek Anthology, which some scholars consider the best in the collection, while others regar (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pamphos
source: Written Πάμφως. Strictly Pamphōs. A mythical poet, who is placed by Pausanias later than Olen, and much earlier than Homer (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pandareos
source: Written Πανδάρεως. Strictly Pandareōs. A son of Merops of Miletus, is said to have stolen the golden dog which Hephaestus had made, from the temple of Zeus in Crete, and to have c (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Panteleus
source: Written Παντέλεος. Strictly Panteleos. The author of nine verses in the Greek Anthology, the first two of which stand in the Vatican MS. as an epigram on Callimachus and Cynageiru (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Parnopius
source: Written Παρυόπιος. Strictly Paryopios. I. e. the expeller of locusts, a surname of Apollo, under which he had a statue on the acropolis at Athens. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Paroreus
source: Written Παρωρεύς. Strictly Parōreus. A son of Tricolonus, and the reputed founder of the town of Paroria in Arcadia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pasidas
source: Written Πασίδας / Πασιάδας. Or PASIADAS, an Achaean, was one of the deputies sent by the Achaeans to Ptolemy Philometor, to congratulate him on his attaining to manhood (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pausiras
source: Written Παυσίρας / Παυσίρις. Or PAUSIRIS (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pedias
source: Written Πεδιάς. A daughter of Menys of Lacedaemon, and the wife of Caranus, king of Attica, from whom an Attic phyle and demos derived their (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pellen
source: Written Πέλλην. Strictly Pellēn. A son of Phorbas and grandson of Triopas, of Argos, was believed by the Argives to have founded the town of Pellene in Achaia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Perperna
source: Written Περπέννας. Strictly Perpennas. Or PERPENNA Περπέννας , the name of a Roman gens (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Perseides
source: Written Περσήϊος. Strictly Persēios. Or PERSEIUS, a patronvylic of Perseus, used to designate his descendants. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Peteos
source: Written Πετεώς. Strictly Peteōs. A son of Orneus, and father of Menestheus, was expelled from Athens by Aegeus, and is said to have gone to Phocis, where he founded the town (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Petines
source: Written Πετίνης. Strictly Petinēs. One of the generals who commanded the Persian army at the passage of the Granicus, B. C. 334 . He was killed in the battle. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Petosiris
source: Written Πετόσιρις. An Egyptian priest and astrologer, who is generally named along with Nechepsos, an Egyptian king (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Petronas
source: Written Πετρωνᾶς / Πέτρων. Strictly Petrōnas. The Alexandrian form of the name Πέτρων (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phacrases
source: Written Φακρασῆς. Strictly Phakrasēs. Several persons of this name are enumerated by Fabricius (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pheraulas
source: Written Φεραύλας. Is introduced by Xenophon, in the Cyropaedeia, as a Persian of humble birth, but a favourite with Cyrus, and distinguished by qualities of b (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phigalus
source: Written Φίγαλος. Strictly Phigalos. One of the sons of Lycaon in Arcadia, is said by Pausanias to have founded the town of Phigalia, though in another passage he is called an a (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Philesias
source: Written Φιλησίας. Strictly Philēsias. A statuary of Eretria, whose age is unknown (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phrynnis
source: Written Φρύννις / Φρῦνις. Or PHRYNIS, a celebrated dithyrambic poet, of the time of the Peloponnesian war, was a native of Mytilene, but flourished at Athens (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phurnutus
source: Written Φουρνούτος. Strictly Phournoutos. Is no other than L. Annaeus Cornutus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phylas
source: Written Φύλας. A king of the Dryopes, was attacked and slain by Heracles, because he had violated the sanctuary of Delphi (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phytalus
source: Written Φύταλος. Strictly Phytalos. An Eleusinian hero, who is said to have kindly received Demeter on her wanderings, and was rewarded by the goddess with a fig-tree (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phyxius
source: Written Φύζιος. Strictly Phyzios. I. e., the god who protects fugitives, occurs as a surname of Zeus in Thessaly (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pistius
source: Written Πίστιος. Strictly Pistios. I. e. the god of faith and fidelity, occurs as a surname of Zeus, and, according to some, answers to the Latin Fidius or Medius Fidius. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pityreus
source: Written Πιτυρεύς. A descendant of Ion and father of Procles, was the last king in Peloponnesus before the invasion of the Dorians. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Plancus
source: Written Πλάγκος. Strictly Plankos. The name of the most distinguished family of the plebeian Munatia gens, is said to have signified a person having flat splay feet without an (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Planudes
source: Written Πλανούδης. Strictly Planoudēs. Surnamed MAXIMUS , was one of the most learned of the Constantinopolitan monks of the last age of the Greek empire, and was greatly distingu (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Platonius
source: Written Πλατώνιος. Strictly Platōnios. A grammarian (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Polieus
source: Written Πολιεύς. "the protector of the city;" a surname of Zeus, under which he had an altar on the acropolis at Athens (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Polycaon
source: Written Πολυκάων. Strictly Polykaōn. A son of Lelex, brother of Myles, and husband of Messene, the daughter of Triopas of Argos (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Poplicola
source: Written Ποπλικόλας. Strictly Poplikolas. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Praxaspes
source: Written Πραξάστης. Strictly Praxastēs. A Persian, who was high in favour with king Cambyses, and acted as his messenger (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Prochorus
source: Written Πρόχορος. Strictly Prokhoros. Works Life of St (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pygmon
source: Written Πύγμων / ΠΥΓΜΩΝ. Strictly Pygmōn. The engraver of a gem in the Florentine Museum, the inscription on which has been variously read ΠΕΙΓΜΟ, ΠΕΠΓΑΜΟΓΥ , and ΠΥΓΜΩΝ , but the la (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pyrander
source: Written Πύρανδος. Strictly Pyrandos. Wrote a work on the history of the Peloponnesus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pyrus
source: Written Πύρος / Πῦρος. Strictly Pyros. Borne by 24 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 499 BC to 450 BC. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Rharias
source: Written Ῥαριάς. A surname of Demeter, which she derived from the Rharian plain in the neighbourhood of Eleusis, the principal seat of her worship. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Rhathines
source: Written Ῥαθίνης. Strictly Rhathinēs. A Persian, was one of the commanders sent by Pharnabazus to aid the Bithynians in opposing the passage of the Cyrean Greeks under Xenophon t (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Rhazes
source: Written Ῥαζῆς. Strictly Rhazēs. The author of a Greek medical treatise Περὶ Λοιμικῆς , which was published at the end of Alexander Trallianus, 1548, fol (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Rhexenor
source: Written Ῥηξήνωρ. Strictly Rhēxēnōr. Two mythical personages, one the father of Chalciope, and the second a son of Nausithous the king of the Phaeacians, and accordingly a broth (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Rhopalus
source: Written Ῥόπαλος. Strictly Rhopalos. A son of Heracles and father of Phaestus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Rhuphinus
source: Written Ῥουφῖνος. Strictly Rhouphinos. Borne by 99 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Sabazius
source: Written Σαβάζιος. Strictly Sabazios. A Phrygian divinity, commonly described as a son of Rhea or Cybele ; but in later times he was identified with the mystic Dionysus, who henc (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Salganeus
source: Written Σαλγανεύς. A surname of Apollo, derived from the town of Salganeus in Boeotia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sandacus
source: Written Σάνδακος. Strictly Sandakos. A son of Astynous, and a grandson of Phaethon (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Satureius
source: Written Σατυρήϊος. Strictly Satyrēios. An artist, whose portrait of Arsinoe in glass is highly praised by Diodorus, in an epigram in the Greek Anthology. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sebrus
source: Written Σέβρος. Strictly Sebros. A son of Hippocoon, was worshipped as a hero at Sparta, where he had an heroumn called Sebrium. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Selinus
source: Written Σελινοῦς. Strictly Selinous. A son of Poseidon, was king of Aegialos and father of Helice. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sibyntius
source: Written Σιβύντιος. Strictly Sibyntios. A reader and a slave of the orator Theodectes of Phaselis, who died before B. C. 333 , was the first slave who professed the art of oratory (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sithon
source: Written Σίθων. Strictly Sithōn. A son of Poseidon and Assa, or of Ares and Achiroe, the daughter of Neilns, was married to the nymph Mendeis, by whom he became the father o (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sogdianus
source: Written Σογδιανός. Strictly Sogdianos. Or SECUNDIA'NUS, as he is called by Ctesias, was one of the illegitimate sons of Artaxerxes I. Longimanus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Somis
source: Written Σῶμις. Strictly Sōmis. The artist who made the bronze statue of Procles the son of Lycastidas, of Andros, an Olympic victor in the boys' wrestling. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sosipater
source: Written Σωσίπαγρος. Strictly Sōsipagros. An Athenian comic poet, of the New, and perhaps also of the Middle Comedy (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Spodius
source: Written Σπόδιος. Strictly Spodios. A surname of Apollo at Thebes, derived from σποδός , ashes, because his altar consisted of the ashes of the victims which had been sacrifice (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Stilicho
source: Written Στιλίχων / Στελίχων. Strictly Stilikhōn. The military ruler of the western empire under honorius, was the son of a Vandal captain of the barbarian auxiliaries of the emperor Valens (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Surenas
source: Written Σουρήνας. Strictly Sourēnas. The general of the Parthians, who defeated Crassus in B. C. 54 . (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tabus
source: Written Τάβος / Τάβαι. Strictly Tabos. A hero in Lydia, from whom the town of Tabae in Lydia was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Taureus
source: Written Ταύρεος. Strictly Taureos. A surname of Poseidon, given to him either because bulls were sacrificed to him, or because he was the divinity that gave greet pasture to b (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Taxiles
source: Written Ταξίλης. Strictly Taxilēs. An Indian prince or king, who reigned over the tract between the Indus and the Hydaspes, at the period of the expedition of Alexander , B. C (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tegeates
source: Written Τεγεάτης. Strictly Tegeatēs. A son of Lycaon, and the reputed founder of Tegea in Arcadia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tegyreius
source: Written Τεγυρήιος / Τέγυρα. Strictly Tegyrēios. A surname of Apollo, derived from the town of Tegyra in Boeotia. where, according to some traditions, the god had been born. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Teleon
source: Written Τελέων. Strictly Teleōn. An Athenian, a son of Ion, the husband of Zeuxippe, and father of the Argonaut Butes. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Temenites
source: Written Τεμενίτης. Strictly Temenitēs. A surname of Apollo, derived from his sacred temenus in the neighbourhood of Syracuse. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tenerus
source: Written Τένερος. Strictly Teneros. A soothsayer, a son of Apolio by Melia, and a brother of Ismenius. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tenes
source: Written Τήννης. Strictly Tēnnēs. Or TENNES, a son of Cycnus, the king of Colone in Troas, and Procleia, or, according to others, a son of Apollo, and brother of Hemithea (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tennes
source: Written Τέννης. Strictly Tennēs. King of Sidon in the revolt of Phoenicia against Artaxerxes III. He betrayed the town to Artaxerxes, but was notwithstanding put to death by (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Terambus
source: Written Τέραμβος. Strictly Terambos. A son of Euseirus and Eidothea (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Teutamias
source: Written Τευταμίας. A king of Larissa in Thessaly, and father of the Pelasgian Lethus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Teutarus
source: Written Τεύταρος. Strictly Teutaros. The original owner of the bow which was used by Heracles. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Thimbron
source: Written Θίμβρων / Θίβρων. Strictly Thimbrōn. Or THIBRON (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Thymondas
source: Written Θυμώνδας. Strictly Thymōndas. A son of MENTOR the Rhodian, and nephew of MEMNON . In B. C. 333 , he was sent down into Lycia by king Dareius to commission Pharnabazus to  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Titias
source: Written Τιτίας. One of the Idaean Dactyls, or according to others, a Mariandynian hero, is called a son of Zeus and Mariandynus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tolynus
source: Written Τόλυνος. Strictly Tolynos. Of Megara, is supposed to have been a comic poet of the Old Comedy, before Cratinus, and about contemporary with Ecphantides, on the authori (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Trambelus
source: Written Τράμβηλος. Strictly Trambēlos. A son of Telamon and Theaneira or Hesione, a king of the Leleges. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tribunus
source: Written Τριβοῦνος. Strictly Tribounos. A very eminent physician, a native of Palestine, and a man of great piety and benevolence (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Triphylus
source: Written Τρίφυλος. Strictly Triphylos. A son of Arcas from whom Tryphylia, a portion of Elis, was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Trophilus
source: Written Τρόφιλος. Strictly Trophilos. A physician quoted by Stobaeus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tros
source: Written Τρώς. Strictly Trōs. A son of Erichthonius and Astyoche, and a grandson of Dardanus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Turnus
source: Written Τοῦρνος. Strictly Tournos. A statuary, known only by the single passage in which Tatian mentions his statue of the courtezan Lais. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tyriaspes
source: Written Τυριάσπης. Strictly Tyriaspēs. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Valerius
source: Written Οὐαλλέριος. Strictly Ouallerios. Artists (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Viriathus
source: Written Οὐιρίαθος. Strictly Ouiriathos. A Lusitanian, commanded his countrymen in their war against the Romans, whose power he defied, and whose armies he vanquished during many su (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

source: Written Ἀργιλεωνίς. Strictly Argileōnis. Mother of Brasidas (Smith's Dictionary). Borne by 1 person in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 480 BC to 420 BC. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Boeo
source: Written Βοιώ. Strictly Boiō. Modern spelling: Beo. An ancient poetess of Delphi, composed a hymn of which Pausanias has preserved four lines (Smith's Dictionary). Borne by 1 person in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 500 BC to 400 BC. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Despoena
source: Written Δέσποινα. Strictly Despoina. Modern spelling: Despena. The ruling goddess or the mistress, occurs as a surname of several divinities, such as Aphrodite (Smith's Dictionary). Borne by 1 person in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 100 AD to 200 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Eudocia
source: Written Εὐδοκία. Strictly Eudokia. Modern spelling: Eudokia. The name of several Byzantine princesses. (Smith's Dictionary). Borne by 1 person in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 500 AD to 600 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Poena
source: Written Ποινή. Strictly Poinē. Modern spelling: Pena. A personification of retaliation, is sometimes mentioned as one being, and sometimes in the plural (Smith's Dictionary). Borne by 1 person in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 100 BC to 100 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Praxidice
source: Written Πραξιδίκη / Πραξιδίκα. Strictly Praxidikē. Modern spelling: Praxidike. I. e. the goddess who carries out the objects of justice, or watches that justice is done to men (Smith's Dictionary). Borne by 1 person in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 550 BC to 501 BC. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Euphrosyna
source: Written Εὐφροσύνα / Εὐφροσύνη. Borne by 149 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Achiroe
source: Written Ἀχιρόη. Strictly Akhiroē. Modern spelling: Achire. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Agnodice
source: Written Ἀγνοδίκη. Strictly Agnodikē. Modern spelling: Agnodike. The name of the earliest midwife mentioned among the Greeks (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Agoraea
source: Written Ἀγοραία / Ἀγοραῖος. Strictly Agoraia. Modern spelling: Agorea. And AGORAEUS, are epithets given to several divinities who were considered as the protectors of the assemblies of the people in the ἀγορά ,  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ambracia
source: Written Ἀμβρακία. Strictly Ambrakia. Modern spelling: Ambrakia. A daughter of Augeas, from whom the town of Ambracia derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Antinoe
source: Written Ἀντινόη. Strictly Antinoē. Modern spelling: Antine. A daughter of Cepheus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Aphacitis
source: Written Ἀφακῖτις. Strictly Aphakitis. Modern spelling: Aphakitis. A surname of Aphrodite, derived from the town of Aphace in Coele-Syria, where she had a celebrated temple with an oracle, which was destroye (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Apotrophia
source: Written Ἀποτροφία. "the expeller," a surname of Aphrodite, under which she was worshipped at Thebes, and which described her as the goddess who expelled from t (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Aricina
source: Written Ἀρικίνη. Strictly Arikinē. Modern spelling: Arikina. A surname of Artemis, derived from the town of Aricia in Latium, where she was worshipped (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bebryce
source: Written Βεβρύκη. Strictly Bebrykē. Modern spelling: Bebryke. One of the Danaids, whom Apollodorus calls Bryce, and from whom the Bebryces in Bithynia were believed to have derived their name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Berecynthia
source: Written Βερεκυνθία. Strictly Berekynthia. A surname of Cybele, which she derived either from mount Berecynthus, or from a fortified place of that name in Phrygia, where she was parti (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Biadice
source: Written Βιαδίκη. Strictly Biadikē. Modern spelling: Biadike. Or, as some MSS. call her, Demodice, the wife of Creteus, who on account of her love for Phrixus meeting with no return, accused him before  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Britomartis
source: Written Βριτόμαρτις. Appears to have originally been a Cretan divinity of hunters and fishermen (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bunaea
source: Written Βουναία. Strictly Bounaia. Modern spelling: Bunea. A surname of Hera, deived from Bunus, the son of Hermes and Alcidameia, who is said to have built a sanctuary to Hera on the road which led  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cassiphone
source: Written Κασσιφόνη. Strictly Kassiphonē. A daughter of Odysseus by Circe, and sister of Telegonus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ceroessa
source: Written Κερόεσσα. Strictly Keroessa. Modern spelling: Ceressa. A daughter of Zeus by Io, and born on the spot where Byzantium was afterwards built (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Chelidonis
source: Written Χελιδονίς. Strictly Khelidonis. A Spartan woman of great beauty and royal blood, daughter of Leotychides (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cidaria
source: Written Κιδαρία. Strictly Kidaria. A surname of the Eleusinian Demeter at Pheneus, in Arcadia, derived either from an Arcadian dance called κίδαρις , or from a royal head-dres (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Coryphaea
source: Written Κορυφαία. Strictly Koryphaia. Modern spelling: Coryphea. The goddess who inhabits the summit of the mountain, a surname of Artemis, under which she had a temple on mount Coryphaeon, near Epidaurus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Coryphasia
source: Written Κορυφασία. Strictly Koryphasia. A surname of Athena, derived from the promontory of Coryphasion, on which she had a sanctuary. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Corythallia
source: Written Κορυθαλλία. Strictly Korythallia. A surname of Artemis at Sparta, at whose festival of the Tithenidia the Spartan boys were carried into her sanctuary. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cranaea
source: Written Κραναῖα. Strictly Kranaia. Modern spelling: Cranea. A surname of Artemis, derived from a temple on a hill near Elateia in Phocis, in which the office of priest was always held by youths below  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Damostratia
source: Written Δαμοστρατία. A courtezan of the emperor Commodus, who subsequently became the wife of Cleander, the favourite of the emperor. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ececheiria
source: Written Ἐκεχειρία. Strictly Ekekheiria. That is, the armistice or truce, which was personified and represented as a divine being at the entrance of the tempie of Zeus at Olympia; t (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Harpalyce
source: Written Ἁρπαλύκη. Strictly Harpalykē. Modern spelling: Harpalyke. A daughter of Harpalycus, king of the Amymnaeans in Thrace (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hecaerge
source: Written Ἑκαέργη. Strictly Hekaergē. Modern spelling: Hecerge. A daughter of Boreas, and one of the Hyperborean maidens, who were believed to have introduced the worship of Artemis in Delos. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Helice
source: Written Ἡλίκη. Strictly Hēlikē. Modern spelling: Helike. A daughter of Lycaon, was beloved by Zeus, but Hera, out of jealousy, metamorphosed her into a she-bear, whereupon Zeus placed her among the (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hercyna
source: Written Ἕρκυνα. Strictly Herkyna. Modern spelling: Herkyna. A divinity of the lower world, respecting whom the following tradition is related (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hipparchia
source: Written Ἱππαρχία. Strictly Hipparkhia. Born at Maroneia, a town of Thrace (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hippocampe

Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Iaeira
source: Written Ἰάειρα. Modern spelling: Ieira. One of the daughters of Nereus and Doris. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ischys
source: Written Ἴσχυς. Strictly Iskhys. Modern spelling: Iskys. A son of Elatus, and the beloved of Coronis at the time when she was with child by Apollo (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Laothoe
source: Written Λαοθόν. Strictly Laothon. Modern spelling: Laothe. A daughter of Altes, king of the Leleges: she became by Priam the mother of Lycaon and Polydorus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Leuconoe
source: Written Λευκονόη. Strictly Leukonoē. Modern spelling: Leucone. A daughter of Poseidon and Themisto. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Leucophryne
source: Written Λευκοφρύνη. Strictly Leukophrynē. A surname of Artemis, derived from the town of Leucophrys in Phrygia, where, as well as at Magnesia on the Maeander, she had a splendid temp (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Melinaea
source: Written Μελιναία. Strictly Melinaia. Modern spelling: Melinea. A surname of Aphrodite, which she derived from the Argive town Meline. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mithridatis
source: Written Μιθριδάτις. A daughter of Mithridates the Great, who had been at one time betrothed to Ptolemy, king of Egypt; but the marriage never took place, and sh (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mycalessia
source: Written Μυκαλησσία. Strictly Mykalēssia. A surname of Demeter, derived from Mycalessus in Boeotia, where the goddess had a sanctuary. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Myrtoessa
source: Written Μυρτώεσσα. Strictly Myrtōessa. Modern spelling: Myrtessa. The nymph of a well of the same name in Arcadia; she was represented at Megalopolis along with Archiroe, Hagno, Anthracia and Nais. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Panachaea
source: Written Πανάχαια. Strictly Panakhaia. Modern spelling: Panachea. That is, the goddess of all the Achaeans, occurs as a surname of Demeter, at Aegae, in Achaia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Penthesilea
source: Written Πενθεσίλεια. Strictly Penthesileia. A daughter of Ares and Otrera, and queen of the Amazons. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pepaepiris
source: Written Πεπαιπιρίς. Strictly Pepaipiris. Modern spelling: Pepepiris. A queen of Bosporus, known only from her coins, from which it appears that she was the wife of Sauromates I. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pessinuntia
source: Written Πεσσινουντία / Πεσσινονντίς. Strictly Pessinountia. A surname of Cybele, which she derived from the town of Pessinus, in Galatia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phaenna
source: Written Φαεννά. Modern spelling: Phenna. One of the Charites. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phanothiea
source: Written Φανοθέα. Strictly Phanothea. Was the wife of the Athenian Icarius. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pharmacea
source: Written Φαρμάκεια. Strictly Pharmakeia. Modern spelling: Pharmakea. The nymph of a well with poisonous powers, near the river Hissus, in Attica; she is described as a playmate of Oreithyia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pharygaea
source: Written Φαρνγαία / Φαρύγαι. Strictly Pharngaia. Modern spelling: Pharygea. A surname of Hera, derived from the town of Pharygae, in Locris, where she had a temple. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phemonoe
source: Written Φημονόη. Strictly Phēmonoē. Modern spelling: Phemone. A mythical Greek poetess of the ante-Homeric period, was said to have been the daughter of Apollo, and his first priestess at Delphi, and th (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pheraea
source: Written Φεραία. Strictly Pheraia. Modern spelling: Pherea. A surname of Artemis at Pherae in Thessaly, at Argos and Sicyon, where she had temples. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Philodamea
source: Written Φιλοδάμεια. Strictly Philodameia. One of the daughters of Danaus, became by Hermes the mother of Pharis. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Philodice
source: Written Φιλοδίκη. Strictly Philodikē. Modern spelling: Philodike. Adaughter of Inachus and the wife of Leucippus, by whom she became the mother of Hilaeira and Phoebe. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Philonoe
source: Written Φιλονίη. Strictly Philoniē. Modern spelling: Philone. The lame of two mythical personages, one a daughter of Tyndareos, who was rendered immortal by Artemis (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Polyboea
source: Written Πολύβοια. Strictly Polyboia. Modern spelling: Polybea. The name of two mythical personages, one a sister of Hiacynthus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Promachorma
source: Written Προμαχόρμα. Strictly Promakhorma. I. e. "the protectress of the bay," was a surname of Athena, under which she had a sanctuary on mount Buporthmos near Hermione. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pronaea
source: Written Προνιάα. Strictly Proniaa. Modern spelling: Pronea. A surname of Athena, under which she had a chapel at Delphi, in front of the temple of Apollo. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pulcheria

D. 414 , and was succe (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Rhoetea
source: Written Ῥοιτεία. Strictly Rhoiteia. Modern spelling: Rhetea. A daughter of the Thracian king Sithon and Achiroe, a daughter of Neilos (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sinoe
source: Written Σινόη. Strictly Sinoē. Modern spelling: Sine. An Arcadian nymph, brought up the god Pan, who derived from her the surname Sinoeis. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sisygambis

name: Sophonisba
source: Written Σοφόνισβα / Σοφόνιβα. A daughter of the Carthaginian general, Hasdrubal, the son of Gisco (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tauropolis
source: Written Ταυρόπολις. A daughter of the Megarian Cleson, who was believed, together with her sister Cleso, to have found and buried the body of Ino, which had bee (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tritaea
source: Written Τρίταια. Strictly Tritaia. Modern spelling: Tritea. A daughter of Triton, a priestess of Athena, by whom Ares became the father of Melanippus, who gave to a town in Achaia the name of his moth (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Zerynthia
source: Written Ζηρυνθία. Strictly Zērynthia. A surname of Aphrodite, from the town of Zerinthus in Thrace, where she had a sanctuary said to have been built by Phaedra. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Zosteria
source: Written Ζωστηρία / Ζωστήρ. Strictly Zōstēria. A surname of Athena among the Epienemidian Locrians. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Zygia
source: Written Ζυγία / Ζυγίος. And ZYGIUS, are surnames of Hera and Zeus, describing them as presiding over marriage. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

source: Written Μενάλιππος / Μελάνιππος. Strictly Menalippos. An architect, probably of Athens, who, in conjunction with the Roman architects, C. and M. name: Aristonous
source: Written Ἀριστόνοος. Strictly Aristonoos. A statuary, a native of Aegina, made a statue of Zeus, which was dedicated by the Metapontines at Olympia. (Smith's Dictionary). source: Written Ἀγχισιάδης. Strictly Ankhisiadēs. A patronymic from Anchises, used to designate his son Aeneas (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 17.754. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Arceisiades

name: Ariabignes

name: Ariomardus
source: Written Ἀριόμαρδος. Strictly Ariomardos. A Persian word, the latter part of which is the same as the Persian merd, whence comes merdi (Smith's Dictionary). In Herodotus 7.67.1. name: Artachaees
source: Written Ἀρταχαίης. Strictly Artakhaiēs. Modern spelling: Artachees. name: Artavasdes
source: Written Ἀρταβάζης / Ἀρταουάσδης / Ἀρταβάσδης. Strictly Artabazēs. ARTAUASDES, or ARTABAZES, called by the Armenian historians, Artawazt (Smith's Dictionary). In Herodotus 1.192.2. name: Aspathines
source: Written Ἀσπαθίνης. Strictly Aspathinēs. One of the seven Persian chiefs, who conspired against the Magi (Smith's Dictionary). In Herodotus 3.70.1. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Boebus
source: Written Βοίβος / Βοίβη. Strictly Boibos. Modern spelling: Bebus. A son of Glaphyrus, from whom the Thessalian town of Boebe derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 2.712. name: Calydonius
source: Written Καλυδώνιος. Strictly Kalydōnios. A surname of Dionysus, whose image was carried from Calydon to Patrae (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 2.6.3. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Cephissus

name: Cleodaeus
source: Written Κλεόδαιος. Strictly Kleodaios. Modern spelling: Cleodeus. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Cychreus
source: Written Κυχρεύς. Strictly Kykhreus. Modern spelling: Cykreus. name: Cynortes
source: Written Κυνόρτης. Strictly Kynortēs. Or CYNORTAS, a son of Amyclas by Diomede, and brother of Hyacinthus (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 1.9.5. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Cytissorus
source: Written Κυτίσσωρος. Strictly Kytissōros. A son of Phrixus and Chalciope or Iophossa. (Smith's Dictionary). In Argonautica 2.1155. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Dercynus

name: Ereuthalion
source: Written Ἐρευθαλίων. Strictly Ereuthaliōn. An Arcadian, who, in the armour of Areithous, which Lycurgus had given him, fought against the Pylians, but was slain by Nestor. (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 4.319. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Eurysaces

name: Eutresites
source: Written Εὐτρησίτης / Εὔτρησις. Strictly Eutrēsitēs. A surname of Apollo, derived from Eutresis, a place between Plataeae and Thespiae, where he had an ancient oracle. (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 2.502. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Gaeeochus

name: Hippodamas
source: Written Ἱπποδάμας. The father of Perimela, the beloved of Achelous. (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 1.7.3. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Hipponicus

(Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 3.9.2. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Hyperasius

name: Poeas

name: Schoeneus

name: Spargapises

name: Stenyclerus

name: Theiodamas

name: Thymoetes

name: Thrasycles

source: Written Πολύστρατος. Strictly Polystratos. Borne by 148 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 999 BC to 310 AD. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Xenotimus
source: Written Ξηνότιμος / Ξενότιμος. Strictly Xenotimos. Borne by 103 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Damaenetus
source: Written Δαμαένετος / Δαμαίνετος. Strictly Damainetos. Modern spelling: Damenetus. Borne by 100 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 525 BC to 310 AD. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Prothoenor
source: Written Προθοήνωρ / Πρωθοήνωρ. Strictly Prōthoēnōr. Modern spelling: Prothenor. A son of Areilycus, was one of the leaders of the Boeotians against Troy, where he was slain by Polydamas. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Philistides
source: Written Φιλιστίδης. Strictly Philistidēs. Borne by 140 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Zoticus
source: Written Ζωτικός. Strictly Zōtikos. Borne by 135 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Philonicus
source: Written Φιλόνικος. Strictly Philonikos. Borne by 134 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 450 BC to 400 AD. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Philodamus
source: Written Φιλόδαμος. Strictly Philodamos. Borne by 133 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 525 BC to 310 AD. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Mucatralis
source: Written Μουκάτραλις. Strictly Moukatralis. Borne by 126 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 31 BC to 402 AD. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).
