name: Nicaeus
source: Written Νίκαιος. Strictly Nikaios. Modern spelling: Niceus. Borne by 117 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Anicetus
source: Written Ἀνίκητος. Strictly Anikētos. Modern spelling: Aniketus. Borne by 111 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 300 BC to 600 AD. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Eleusinius
source: Written Ἐλευσίνιος. Strictly Eleusinios. Borne by 107 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 200 BC to 325 AD. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Nicetes
source: Written Νικήτης. Strictly Nikētēs. Modern spelling: Niketes. Borne by 105 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Mucianus
source: Written Μουκιανός. Strictly Moukianos. Modern spelling: Mukianus. Borne by 100 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 31 BC to 500 AD. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Abantiades
source: Written Ἀβαντιάδης. Strictly Abantiadēs. Signifies in general a descendant of Abas, but is used especially to designate Perseus, the great-grandson of Abas (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Abrettenus
source: Written Ἀβρεττηνός. Strictly Abrettēnos. A surname of Zeus in Mysia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Abronychus
source: Written Ἀβρώνυχος. Strictly Abrōnykhos. The son of Lysicles, an Athenian, was stationed at Thermopylae with a vessel to communicate between Leonidas and the fleet at Artemisium (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Acacesius
source: Written Ἀκακήσιος. Strictly Akakēsios. Modern spelling: Acakesius. A surname of Hermes (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Acichorius
source: Written Ἀκιχώριος. Strictly Akikhōrios. Was one of the leaders of the Gauls, who invaded Thrace and Macedonia in B. C. 280 . He and Brennus commanded the division that marched into (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Acoetes
source: Written Ἀκοίτης. Strictly Akoitēs. Modern spelling: Acetes. According to Ovid (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Acraepheus
source: Written Ἀκραιφεύς / Ἀκραιφία. Strictly Akraipheus. Modern spelling: Acrepheus. A son of Apollo, to whom the foundation of the Boeotian town of Acraephia was ascribed (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Acroeites
source: Written Ἀκρωρείτης / Ἀκρωρεία. Strictly Akrōreitēs. Modern spelling: Acreites. A surname of Dionysus, under which he was worshipped at Sicyon, and which is synonymous with Eriphius, under which name he was worshipped at (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Agathyrnus
source: Written Ἀγάθυπνος. Strictly Agathypnos. A son of Acolus, regarded as the founder of Agathyrnum in Sicily. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Agraeus
source: Written Ἀγραῖος. Strictly Agraios. Modern spelling: Agreus. The hunter, a surname of Apollo (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Alcithus
source: Written Ἄλκιθος. Strictly Alkithos. Modern spelling: Alkithus. Sent as ambassador by the Achaeans to Ptolemy Philometor, B. C. 169 , when they heard that the Anacleteria were to be celebrated in his hono (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Amarynthus
source: Written Ἀμάρυνθος. Strictly Amarynthos. A hunter of Artemis, from whom the town of Amarynthus in Euboea (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Amoraeus
source: Written Ἀμοραῖος. Strictly Amoraios. Modern spelling: Amoreus. King of the Derbicae, in a war against whom, according to Ctesias (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Anchesmius
source: Written Ἀγχέδμιος. Strictly Ankhedmios. A surname of Zeus derived from the hill Anchesmus in Attica, on which, as on several Attic hills, there was a statue of the god. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Aneroestus
source: Written Ἀνηρόεστος / Ἀνηροέστης. Strictly Anēroestos. Modern spelling: Anerestus. Or ANEROESTES, king of the Gaesati, a Gallic people between the Alps and the Rhone, who was induced by the Boii and the Insubres to make war (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Anthaeus
source: Written Ἀνθαῖος. Strictly Anthaios. Modern spelling: Antheus. Or Antaeus, a physician, whose ridiculous and superstitious remedy for hydrophobia is mentioned by Pliny. One of his prescriptions is preser (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Apesantius
source: Written Ἀπεσάντιος. Strictly Apesantios. A surname of Zeus, under which he had a temple on mount Apesas near Nemea, where Perseus was said to have first offered sacrifices to him. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Aracynthias
source: Written Ἀρακυνθιάς / Ἀράκυνθος. Strictly Arakynthias. A surname of Aphrodite, derived from mount Aracynthus, the position of which is a matter of uncertainty, and on which she had a temple. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Archimelus
source: Written Ἀρχίμηλος. Strictly Arkhimēlos. The author of an epigram on the great ship of Hiero, which appears to have been built about 220 B. C. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Aribaeus
source: Written Ἀρίβαιος. Strictly Aribaios. Modern spelling: Aribeus. The king of the Cappadocians, was slain by the Hyrcanians, in the time of the elder Cyrus, according to Xenophon's Cyropaedia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Artoces
source: Written Ἀρτώκης. Strictly Artōkēs. Modern spelling: Artokes. King of the Iberians, against whom Pompey marched in B. C. 65 . Pompey crossed the Cyrnus and defeated Artoces; and when he also crossed the (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Asbamaeus
source: Written Ἀσβαμαῖος. Strictly Asbamaios. Modern spelling: Asbameus. A surname of Zeus, the protector of the sanctity of oaths (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ascalaphus
source: Written Ἀσκάλοφος. Strictly Askalophos. A son of Ares and Astyoche, and brother of Ialmenus, together with whom he led the Minyans of Orchomenos against Troy, in thirty ships. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Axiopoenos
source: Written Ἀξιόποινος. Strictly Axiopoinos. Modern spelling: Axiopenos. The avenger, a surname of Athena (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Baccheidas
source: Written Βακχείδας. Strictly Bakkheidas. Modern spelling: Backeidas. Of Sicyon, a dancer and teacher of music, in honour of whom there is an ancient epigram of four lines preserved by Athenaeus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Baeton
source: Written Βαίτων. Strictly Baitōn. Modern spelling: Beton. Was employed by Alexander the Great in measuring distances in his marches, whence he is called ὁ Ἀλεξάνδρου βηματιστής . Works σταθμοί τῆς Ἀ (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bagistanes
source: Written Βαγιστάνης. Strictly Bagistanēs. A distinguished Babylonian, deserted Bessus and the conspirators, when Alexander was in pursuit of them and Dareius, B. C. 330 , and informe (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Barsaentes
source: Written Βαρσαέντης / Βαρζάεντος. Strictly Barsaentēs. Modern spelling: Barsentes. Or BARZAENTUS, satrap of the Arachoti and Drangae, was present at the battle of Guagamela, B. C. 331 , and after the defeat of the Persian a (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bathanatius
source: Written Βαθανάτιος. Strictly Bathanatios. The leader of the Cordistae, a Gaulish tribe, who invaded Greece with Brennus in B. C. 279 . After the defeat of Brennus, Bathanatius led hi (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bemarchius
source: Written Βημάρχιος. Strictly Bēmarkhios. A Greek sophist and rhetorician of Caesareia in Cappadocia, who lived in or shortly after the time of the emperor Constantine, whose history (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Besantinus
source: Written Βησαντῖνος. Strictly Bēsantinos. The Vatican MS. of the Greek Anthology attributes to an author of this name two epigrams, of which one is also ascribed to Pallas (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bocchoris
source: Written Βόκχορις. Strictly Bokkhoris. Modern spelling: Bockoris. An Egyptian king and legislator, who was distinguished for his wisdom, avarice, and bodily weakness (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Bocchus
source: Written Βόκχος. Strictly Bokkhos. Modern spelling: Bockus. A king of Mauretania, who acted a prominent part in the war of the Romans against Jugurtha (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Boedromius
source: Written Βοηδρόμιος. Strictly Boēdromios. Modern spelling: Bedromius. The helper in distress, a surname of Apollo at Athens, the origin of which is explained in different ways (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Boeus
source: Written Βοιός. Strictly Boios. Modern spelling: Beus. A son of Heracles, and founder of the Laconian town of Boeae, to which he led colonists from Etis, Aphrodisias, and Side. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Botthaeus
source: Written Βοτθαιός. Strictly Botthaios. Modern spelling: Bottheus. Is mentioned along with Scylax of Caryanda by Marcianus of Heracleia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Brachylles
source: Written Βραχύλλης / Βραχύλλας. Strictly Brakhyllēs. Or BRACHYLLAS, was the son of Neon, a Boeotian, who studiously courted the favour of the Macedonian king Antigonus Doson; and accordingly, w (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Brisaeus
source: Written Βρισαῖος / Βρίσα. Strictly Brisaios. Modern spelling: Briseus. A surname of Dionysus, derived from mount Brisa in Lesbos (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Brunichius
source: Written Βρουνίχιος. Strictly Brounikhios. A chronographer of uncertain date, referred to by Joannes Malala (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Callipygos
source: Written Καλλίπυγος. Strictly Kallipygos. A surname of Aphrodite, of which the origin is related by Athenaeus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Carsignatus
source: Written Καρσίγνατος. Strictly Karsignatos. A Galatian prince, who was at one time allied with Pharnaces (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cataebates
source: Written Καταιβάτης. Strictly Kataibatēs. Modern spelling: Catebates. Occurs as a surname of several gods (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Catharsius
source: Written Καθάρσιος. Strictly Katharsios. The purifyer or atoner, a surname of Zeus, under which he in conjunction with Nice had a temple at Olympia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cebren
source: Written Κεβρήν. Strictly Kebrēn. A river-god in Troas, the father of Asterope or Hesperie and Oenone. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ceceides
source: Written Κηκείδης. Strictly Kēkeidēs. Modern spelling: Cekeides. Of Hermione, a very ancient Greek dithyrambic poet, whom Aristophanes (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Celeus
source: Written Κηλεός. Strictly Kēleos. A king of Eleusis, and husband of Metaneira (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cephren
source: Written Κεφρήν. Strictly Kephrēn. Is the name, according to Diodorus, of the Egyptian king whom Herodotus calls Chephren (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ceryx
source: Written Κήρυξ. Strictly Kēryx. An Attic hero, a son of Hermes and Aglauros, from whom the priestly family of the Cervces at Athens derived their origin. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Choricius
source: Written Χορίκιος. Strictly Khorikios. Modern spelling: Chorikius. A rhetorician and sophist of Gaza, the pupil of Procopius of Gaza, and afterwards of another sophist of the same place, flourished in the re (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cinaethus
source: Written Κίναιθος. Strictly Kinaithos. Modern spelling: Cinethus. Or CYNAETHUS, of Chios, a rhapsodist, who was generally supposed by the ancients to have been the author of the Homeric hymn to Apollo (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cios
source: Written Κῖος. Strictly Kios. A son of Olympus, from whom Cios on the Propontis derived its name, as he was believed to have led thither a band of colonists from Miletus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Colaenis
source: Written Κολαινίς. Strictly Kolainis. Modern spelling: Colenis. A surname of Artemis in the Attic demos of Myrrhinus, was derived from a mythical king, Colaenus, who was believed to have reigned even befo (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Colchas
source: Written Κόλχας / Κολίχας. Strictly Kolkhas. Modern spelling: Colkas. Or CO'LICHAS, a petty prince of Spain, who ruled over twentyeight cities, and furnished supplies of troops to Scipio against Mago and Hasdru (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Concolerus
source: Written Κογκόλερος / Κονοδκογκόλοπος. Strictly Konkoleros. The Greek name of Sardanapalus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Croceatas
source: Written Κροκεάτας. Strictly Krokeatas. Modern spelling: Crokeatas. A surname of Zeus, derived from a place, Croceae, near Gythium in Laconia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cyllen
source: Written Κυλλήν. Strictly Kyllēn. A son of Elatus, from whom mount Cyllene in Arcadia was believed to have received its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cynurus
source: Written Κύνουρος. Strictly Kynouros. A son of Perseus, who is said to have led colonists from Argos into Cynuria, a valley between Argolis and Laconia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Dataphernes
source: Written Δαταφέρνης. Strictly Dataphernēs. A Persian in the confidence of Bessus, and one of those who betrayed him to Alexander , B. C. 329 . He joined Spitamenes, satrap of Sogdiana (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Diaethus
source: Written Δίαιθος. Strictly Diaithos. Modern spelling: Diethus. The author of commentaries on the Homeric poems, which seem to have been chiefly of an historical nature, and are referred to in the Venetia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Dictaeus
source: Written Δικταῖος. Strictly Diktaios. Modern spelling: Dicteus. A surname of Zeus, derived from mount Dicte in the eastern part of Crete (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Diopeithes
source: Written Διοπρείθης. Strictly Diopreithēs. A half-fanatic, half-impostor, who made at Athens an apparently thriving trade of oracles (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Dioscurides
source: Written Διοσουρίδης. Strictly Diosouridēs. Or DIOSCO'RIDES. 1. Of Samos, the maker of two mosaic pavements found at Pompeii, in the so-called villa of Cicero (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Diotogenes
source: Written Διοτογένης. Strictly Diotogenēs. A Pythagorean philosopher, who wrote a work πεπὶ ὁσιότητος , of which three fragments are preserved in Stobaeus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Dysponteus
source: Written Δυσποντεύς / Δυσπόντιος. Or DYSPO'NTIUS, according to Pausanias, a son of Oenomaus, but according to Stephanus of Byzantium, a son of Pelops, was believed to be the  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ecebolius
source: Written Ἑκηβόλιος. Strictly Hekēbolios. Modern spelling: Ekebolius. A sophist of Constantinople, who in the reign of Constantine the Great pretended to be a Christian, but afterwards, in the time of the emper (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Eleuthereus
source: Written Ἐλευθερεύς. A surname of Dionysus, which he derived either from Eleuther, or the Boeotian town of Eleutherae; but it may also be regarded as equivalent  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Emmenidae
source: Written Ἐμμενίδαι. Strictly Emmenidai. Modern spelling: Emmenide. A princely family at Agrigentum, which traced its origin to the mythical hero Polyneices (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Endoeus
source: Written Ἔνδοιος. Strictly Endoios. Modern spelling: Endeus. An Athenian statuary, is called a disciple of Daedalus, whom he is said to have accompanied when he fled to Crete (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Epactaeus
source: Written Ἐπακταῖος / Ἐπάκτιος. Strictly Epaktaios. Modern spelling: Epacteus. Or EPA'CTIUS, that is, the god worshipped on the coast, was used as a surname of Poseidon in Samos, and of Apollo. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Eugesippus
source: Written Εὐγήσιππος. Strictly Eugēsippos. An author who lived about A. D. 1040 , but no particulars are known about him (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Euphiletus
source: Written Εὐφίλητος. Strictly Euphilētos. Borne by 99 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Euphronides
source: Written Εὐφρονίδης. Strictly Euphronidēs. Of Corinth, a Greek grammarian, who is mentioned among the teachers of Aristophanes of Byzantium. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Eurysternos
source: Written Εὐρύστερνος. That is, the goddess with a broad chest, is a surname of Ge (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Euxenidae
source: Written Εὐξενίδαι. Strictly Euxenidai. Modern spelling: Euxenide. A noble family among the Aeginetans, celebrated by Pindar in his ode in honour of one of its members, Sogenes, who was victorious in the boy (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Gabaeus
source: Written Γαβαῖος. Strictly Gabaios. Modern spelling: Gabeus. Ruler of the Lesser or Hellespontine Phrygia, is mentioned by Xenophon (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Galinthias
source: Written Γαλινθιάς. Or, as Ovid (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Graecus
source: Written Γραῖκος / Γραικός / Γραικοί. Strictly Graikos. Modern spelling: Grecus. A son of Thessalus, from whom the Greeks derived the name of Γραικοί (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Gregentius
source: Written Γρηγέντιος. Strictly Grēgentios. Archbishop of Tephar, capital of the Homeritae, a nation of Arabia Felix, the site of which is a little above 100 miles N.N.W. of Aden (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hegesippus
source: Written Ἠγήσιππος. Strictly Ēgēsippos. An Athenian of the time of Demosthenes, and the brother of Hegesander, was nicknamed Κρωβύλος by Aeschines, but for what reason is quite unc (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Heliadae
source: Written Ἡλιάδαι. Strictly Hēliadai. Modern spelling: Heliade. And HELIADES, that is, the male and female descendants of Helios, and might accordingly be applied to all his children, but in mythology the (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hellanicus
source: Written Ἑλλάνικος. Strictly Hellanikos. Of Mytilene in the island of Lesbos, the most eminent among the Greek logographers (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Heracleonas
source: Written Ἡρακλειωνᾶς. Strictly Hērakleiōnas. The second son of the emperor Heraclius, reigned together with his brother, Constantine III., after the death of their father in March, A. D (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hermagoras
source: Written Ἑρμαγόρας. Of Temnos, a distinguished Greek rhetorician of the time of Pompey and Cicero (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hermanubis
source: Written Ἑρμανοῦβις. Strictly Hermanoubis. A son of Osiris and Nephthys, was represented as a human being with a dog's head, and regarded as the symbol of the Egyptian priesthood, eng (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hermarchus
source: Written Ἕρμαρχος. Strictly Hermarkhos. Sometimes, but incorrectly, written IIermachus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hermodorus
source: Written Ἑρμόδωρος. Strictly Hermodōros. Of Ephesus, a person of great distinction, but was expelled by his fellow-citizens, for which Heracleitus censured them very severely. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Herodianus
source: Written Ἡρωδιανός. Strictly Hērōdianos. A writer on Roman history (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Herophilus
source: Written Ἡρόφιλος. Strictly Hērophilos. One of the most celebrated physicians of antiquity, who is best known on account of his skill in anatomy and physiology, but of whose person (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hestiaeus
source: Written Ἑστιαῖος. Strictly Hestiaios. Modern spelling: Hestieus. A native of Perinthus, mentioned by Diogenes Laertius as one of the disciples of Plato. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hetaereius
source: Written Ἑταιρεῖος. Strictly Hetaireios. Modern spelling: Hetereius. The protector of companies or associations of friends, a surname of Zeus, to whom Jason was believed to have offered the first sacrifices, w (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hicesius
source: Written Ἱκέσιος. Strictly Hikesios. Modern spelling: Hikesius. A writer quoted by Clement of Alexandria, as having written a work concerning mysteries, in which he treated incidentally of the religion of (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hieramenes
source: Written Ἱεραμένης. Strictly Hieramenēs. Is name with Tissaphernes and the sons of Pharnaces, as contracting parties to the third treaty between Sparta and Persia, and must therefor (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hierophilus
source: Written Ἱερόφιλος. Strictly Hierophilos. A name which has been supposed by Marx (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hierotheus
source: Written Ἱερόθεος. Strictly Hierotheos. Works Περὶ τῆς Θείας καὶ Ἱερᾶς Τέχνης , De Divina et Sacra Arte He was the author of a Greek poem, consisting of 233 barbarous Iambic lines  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Himeraeus
source: Written Ἱμεραῖος. Strictly Himeraios. Modern spelling: Himereus. Of the borough of Phalerus in Attica, was son of Phanostratus, and brother of the celebrated Demetrius Phalereus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hippagoras
source: Written Ἱππαγόρας. A writer mentioned by Athenaeus as the author of a treatise Περὶ τῆς Καρχηδονίων Πολιτείας . (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hipparinus
source: Written Ἱππαρῖνος. Strictly Hipparinos. A Syracusan, father of Dion (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hippobotus
source: Written Ἱππόβοτος. Strictly Hippobotos. A writer very frequently quoted by Diogenes Laertius (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hippodamus
source: Written Ἱππόδαμος. Strictly Hippodamos. Ἱππόδαμος : the etymological origin of the name is no doubt the same as that of the Homeric word ἱππόδαμος , which so frequently occurs as a (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hipponoidas
source: Written Ἱππονοίδας. A Spartan officer under Agis II., in the battle fought at Mantineia against the Argives and their allies, B. C. 418 . He was accused of cowa (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Homagyrius
source: Written Ὁμαγύριος. Strictly Homagyrios. I.e. the god of the assembly or league, a surname of Zeus, under which he was worshipped at Aegium, on the northwestern coast of Peloponnesu (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Homoloeus
source: Written Ὁμολωεύς. Strictly Homolōeus. Modern spelling: Homoleus. A son of Amphion, from whom the Homoloian gate of Thebes was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hopladamos
source: Written Ὁπλάδαμος. One of the Gigantes who accompanied and protected Rhea when she was on the point of giving birth to Zeus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Horcius
source: Written Ὅρκιος. Strictly Horkios. Modern spelling: Horkius. The god who watches over oaths, or is invoked in oaths, and punishes their violation, occurs chiefly as a surname of Zeus, under which the g (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hyperbatas
source: Written Ὑπερβατᾶς. Or HYPE'RBATUS (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hyperbolus
source: Written Ὑπέρβολος. Strictly Hyperbolos. The Athenian demagogue, was, according to Androtion, son of Antiphanes; according to Theopompus, son of Chremes, and brother of Charon. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hyperechius
source: Written Ὑπερέχιος. Strictly Hyperekhios. Ammianus Marcellinus mentions an officer of this name who commanded a body of troops sent by Procopius to oppose the forces of the emperor V (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hyperochus
source: Written Ὑπέροχος. Strictly Hyperokhos. The generally acknowledged author of a metricalaccount of Cumae, mentioned by Athenaeus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hypsicrates
source: Written Ὑψικράτης. Strictly Hypsikratēs. An historical writer, who wrote an account of Phoenicia in the Phoenician language, which was translated into Greek by a man named Ἄσιτος ,  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Intaphernes
source: Written Ἰνταφέρνης. Strictly Intaphernēs. One of the seven conspirators against the two Magi, who usurped the Persian throne upon the death of Cambyses (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Iphicianus
source: Written Ἰφικιανός. Strictly Iphikianos. A physician, who is mentioned four times by Galen, and whose name is in each passage spelt differently, viz. Ἰφικιανός (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Isodaetes
source: Written Ἰσοδαίτης. Strictly Isodaitēs. Modern spelling: Isodetes. From δαίω , i. e. the god who distributes his gifts equally to all, occurs as a surname of Dionysus Zagreus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Labdacidae
source: Written Λαβδακίδαι. Strictly Labdakidai. Modern spelling: Labdacide. A patronymic from Labdacus, and frequently used not only to designate his children, but his descendants in general, and is therefore applied (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Labrandeus
source: Written Λαβρανδεύς. A surname of Zeus Stratius, which he derived from a temple he had at Labranda. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lacedas
source: Written Λακήδας. Strictly Lakēdas. Modern spelling: Lakedas. Or, as Herodotus calls him, Leocedes, a king of Argos, and father of Melas, is reckoned to have been a descendant of Medon in the fifth gene (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lacinius
source: Written Λακίνιος. Strictly Lakinios. Modern spelling: Lakinius. An Italian hero and fabulous robber, by whom Heracles, on his expedition in Italy, is said to have been robbed of some of the oxen of Geryon (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Laphraeus
source: Written Λαφραῖος. Strictly Laphraios. Modern spelling: Laphreus. A surname of Apollo at Calydon. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Larissaeus
source: Written Λαρισσαῖος / Λαρισσαῖα. Strictly Larissaios. Modern spelling: Larisseus. And LARISSAEA, surnames of Zeus and Apollo, derived from the arx Larissa at Argos (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lexiphanes
source: Written Λεξιφάνης. Strictly Lexiphanēs. An Athenian comic poet, quoted by Alciphron (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Loemius
source: Written Λοίμιος / Λοιμός. Strictly Loimios. Modern spelling: Lemius. The deliverer from plague, was a surname of Apollo at Lindus in Rhodes. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lucillius
source: Written Λουκίλλιος / Λούκιλλος. Strictly Loukillios. Modern spelling: Lukillius. Λουκίλλιος . A poet of the Greek Anthology, who edited two books of epigrams (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Maccabaei
source: Written Μακκαβαῖοι. Strictly Makkabaioi. Modern spelling: Maccabei. The name generally given to the descendants of the family of the heroic Judas Maccabi or Maccabaeus, a surname which he obtained from his gl (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Machaereus
source: Written Μαχαιρεύς. Strictly Makhaireus. Modern spelling: Machereus. I. e. the swordsman, a son of Daetas of Delphi, who is said to have slain Neoptolemus, the son of Achilles, in a quarrel about the sacrifici (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Maemactes
source: Written Μαιμάκτης. Strictly Maimaktēs. Modern spelling: Memactes. I. e. the stormy, a surname of Zeus, from which the name of the Attic month Maemacterion was derived (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Maenalius
source: Written Μαινάλιος. Strictly Mainalios. Modern spelling: Menalius. Or MAENA'LIDES, a surname of Pan, derived from mount Maenalus in Arcadia, which was sacred to the god. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Marmarinus
source: Written Μαρμάρινος. Strictly Marmarinos. I.e. the god of marble, a surname of Apollo, who had a sanctuary in the marble quarries at Carystus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mazaces
source: Written Μαζάκης. Strictly Mazakēs. Modern spelling: Mazakes. A Persian, satrap of Egypt (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mebarsapes
source: Written Μηβαρσάπης. Strictly Mēbarsapēs. King of Adiabene, a province of Assyria, was attacked by Trajan in his expedition against the Parthians. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Megabernes
source: Written Μεγαβέρνης. Strictly Megabernēs. A grandson of Astvages, according to the account of Ctesias. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Melisander
source: Written Μελίσανδρος. Strictly Melisandros. Of Miletus, is said to have written an account of the battles of the Lapithae and Centaurs, and is classed by Aelian with the poets Oroebant (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Micipsa
source: Written Μικίψας. Strictly Mikipsas. Modern spelling: Mikipsa. King of Numidia, was the eldest of the sons of Masinissa who survived their father (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Moiragetes
source: Written Μοιραγέτης. Strictly Moiragetēs. The guide or leader of fate, occurs as a surname of Zeus and Apollo at Delphi. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Monaeses
source: Written Μοναίσης. Strictly Monaisēs. Modern spelling: Moneses. One of the most distinguished men in Parthia in the time of Antony, the triumvir, is spoken of in Vol (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Monoecus
source: Written Μόνοικος. Strictly Monoikos. Modern spelling: Monecus. A surname of Heracles, signifying the god who lives solitary, perhaps because he alone was worshipped in the temples dedicated to him. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Nabarzanes
source: Written Ναβαρζάνης. Strictly Nabarzanēs. A Persian in the service of Dareits (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Nabonassar
source: Written Ναβονάσαρος. Strictly Nabonasaros. Among the most perplexing questions of Eastern history, is the comparative state of the Assyrian and the Babylonian or Chaldean empire, and  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Narcaeus
source: Written Ναρκαῖος. Strictly Narkaios. Modern spelling: Narceus. A son of Dionysus and Narcaea, established a sanctuary of Athena Narcaea in Elis, and also introduced there the worship of Dionysus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Odoacer
source: Written Ὀδόακρος. Strictly Odoakros. Modern spelling: Odoaker. King of Italy, from A. D. 476 - 493 . He was the son of one Edeco, who was undoubtedly the same Edecon who was minister of Attila and his am (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Onaethus
source: Written Ὄναιθος. Strictly Onaithos. Modern spelling: Onethus. A statuary of unknown time and country, who, with his brother Thylacus and their sons, made the statue of Zeus, which the Megarians dedicate (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Oncaeus
source: Written Ὀγκαῖος. Strictly Onkaios. Modern spelling: Onceus. A surname of Apollo, derived from Onceiusm on the river Ladon in Arcadia, where he had a temple. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Panthoedus
source: Written Πανθοίδος. Strictly Panthoidos. Modern spelling: Panthedus. A dialectic philosopher about B. C. 270 , who wrote a treatise, πεοὶ ἀμφιβολιῶν ,, which was attacked by Chrysippus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Parnethius
source: Written Παρνήθιος. Strictly Parnēthios. A surname of Zeus, derived from Mount Parnes in Attica, on which there was a bronze statue of the god. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pelagonius
source: Written Πελαγώνιος. Strictly Pelagōnios. A writer on veterinary surgery (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Peraethus
source: Written Πέραιθος. Strictly Peraithos. Modern spelling: Perethus. A son of Lycaon, from whom the town of Peraetheis in Arcadia was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phaemon
source: Written Φαίμων. Strictly Phaimōn. Modern spelling: Phemon. Works On the Right Management of Dogs Editions (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pharacidas
source: Written Φαρακίδας. Strictly Pharakidas. A Lacedaemonian who commanded a fleet of thirty ships sent by the Spartans and their allies to the assistance of the elder Dionysius, when S (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pharandates
source: Written Φαρανδάτης. Strictly Pharandatēs. Φαρανδάτης a Persian, son of Teaspes, commanded the Marians and Colchians in the expedition of Xerxes against Greece. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pharasmanes
source: Written Φαραδμάνης. Strictly Pharadmanēs. A king of the Scythian tribe of the Chorasmians, who presented himself to Alexander the Great at Zariaspa, B. C. 328 , with friendly offers, (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pharnaspes
source: Written Φαρνάσπης. Strictly Pharnaspēs. A Persian, of the family of the Achaemenidae, was the father of Cassandane, a favourite wife of Cyrus the Great. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pharnuchus
source: Written Φαρνοῦχος. Strictly Pharnoukhos. An historian of uncertain date, who wrote a history of Persia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pheretiades
source: Written Φερητιάδης. Strictly Pherētiadēs. I.e. a son of Pheres (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phileumenos
source: Written Φιλεύμενος. A sculptor, whose name was for the first time discovered in 1808. in an inscription on the support of the left foot of a statue in the Villa (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phillatius
source: Written Φιλλάτιος / Φιλτάτιος. Strictly Phillatios. A grammarian, contemporary with the historian Olympiodorus, about A. D. 407 . Photius in his epitome of Olympio dorus, mentions him as havin (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phrasaortes
source: Written Φρασαόρτης. Strictly Phrasaortēs. Son of Rheomithres, a Persian, who was appointed by Alexander the Great satrap of the province of Persia Proper, B. C. 331 . He died during  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Plemnaeus
source: Written Πλημναῖος. Strictly Plēmnaios. Modern spelling: Plemneus. A son of Peratus in Aegialeia, was the father of Orthopolis whom Demeter reared, all the other children of Plemnaeus having died immediately (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Plesimachus
source: Written Πλησίμαχος. Strictly Plēsimakhos. The writer of Νόστοι (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Polybiades
source: Written Πολυβιάδης. Strictly Polybiadēs. A Lacedaemonian general, succeeded Agesipolis in the command of the army against Olynthus, and compelled the city to surrender in B. C. 379  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Promathides
source: Written Προμαθίδης. Strictly Promathidēs. Of Heracleia, wrote a work entitled Ἡμίαμβοι , which treated of mythological subjects (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pygmaeus
source: Written Πυγμαῖος. Strictly Pygmaios. Modern spelling: Pygmeus. A being whose length is a πυγμὴ , that is, from the elbow to the hand. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Rheomithres
source: Written Ῥεομίθρης. Strictly Rheomithrēs. A Persian who joined in the general revolt of the western provinces from Artaxerxes Mnemon, in B. C. 362 , and was employed by his confedera (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sabaces
source: Written Σαβάκης. Strictly Sabakēs. Modern spelling: Sabakes. A Persian, was satrap of Egypt under Dareius III., and was slain at the battle of Issus, in B. C. 333 (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Scephrus
source: Written Σκέφρος. Strictly Skephros. Modern spelling: Skephrus. A son of Tegeates and Maera, and brother of Leimon (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Scythianus
source: Written Σκυθιανός. Strictly Skythianos. A Manichaean heretic, who, according to Epiphanius, supported his opinions by the philosophy of Pythagoras. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Superianus
source: Written Σουπεριανός. Strictly Souperianos. A sophist at Athens, of whom an account is preserved by Suidas. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Taraxippus
source: Written Ταράξιππος. Strictly Taraxippos. Was the name of a particular spot in the race-course at Olympia, where horses often became shy and frightened (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tarchetius
source: Written Ταρχήτιος. Strictly Tarkhētios. A mythical king of Alba, who in some traditions is connected with the founders of Rome (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tarquinius
source: Written Ταρκύνιος. Strictly Tarkynios. The name of a family in early Roman history, to which the fifth and seventh kings of Rome belonged (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Telchin
source: Written Τελχίν. Strictly Telkhin. Modern spelling: Telkin. A son of Europs, and father of Apis, was king of Sicyon (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Telmissius
source: Written Τελμίσσιος. Strictly Telmissios. A surname of Apollo derived from the Lycian town of Telnissus or Telmessus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Theodoricus
source: Written Θευδέριχος. Strictly Theuderikhos. Or THEODERICUS, surnamed the GREAT, king of the Ostrogoths, was the son of Theodemir by his favourite concubine Eralieva (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Theodotius
source: Written Θεοδότιος. Strictly Theodotios. The author of a medical formula, quoted by Alexander Trallianus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Theoxenius
source: Written Θεοξένιος. Strictly Theoxenios. A surname of Apollo and Hermes. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tiboetes
source: Written Τιβοίτης. Strictly Tiboitēs. Modern spelling: Tibetes. An uncle of Prusias I., king of Bithynia, was living in Macedonia in the early part of the reign of Prusias, and was sent for by the Byzanti (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tithraustes
source: Written Τιθραύστης. Strictly Tithraustēs. A Persian, who was commissioned by Artaxerxes II., in B. C. 395 , to put Tissaphernes to death, and to succeed him in his satrapy (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Tricolonus
source: Written Τρικόλωνος. Strictly Trikolōnos. Two mythical personages, one a son of Lycaon, and founder of Tricoloni in Arcadia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Zarbienus
source: Written Ζαρβιηνός. Strictly Zarbiēnos. King of Gordyene, made overtures to Appius Claudius, when the latter was staying at Antiocheia, wishing to shake off the yoke of Tigranes (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Zarex
source: Written Ζάρηξ. Strictly Zarēx. A hero who was believed to have been instructed in music by Apollo, and had an heroum near Eleusis (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Zariadres
source: Written Ζαριάδρης. Strictly Zariadrēs. The younger brother of Hystaspes, was the hero of the celebrated love-story of Zariadres and Odatis. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Zarzas
source: Written Ζάρζας / Ζάρξας. Or ZARXAS, a Libyan, commander of a portion of the mercenary troops which revolted from the Carthaginians (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Zeneus
source: Written Ζηνεύς / Ζηνίς. Strictly Zēneus. Or ZENIS, of Chios wrote a work on his native country. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Zoroaster
source: Written Ζωροάστρης. Strictly Zōroastrēs. Or ZOROASTRES, the ZARATHUSTRA of the Zendavesta, and the ZERDUSHT of the Persians, was the founder of the Magian religion (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

source: Written Αἴθουσα. Strictly Aithousa. A daughter of Poseidon and Alcyone, who was beloved by Apollo, and bore to him Eleuther. (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 3.10.1. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Hegesipyla
source: Written Ἡγησιπύλη. Strictly Hēgēsipylē. Daughter of Olorus, king of Thrace, and wife of Miltiades (Smith's Dictionary). In Herodotus 6.39.2. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Onca
source: Written Ὄγκα. Strictly Onka. A surname of Athena, which she derived from the town of Oncae in Boeotia, where she had a sanctuary. (Smith's Dictionary). In Seven against Thebes 163. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Phoronis
source: Written Φορωνίς. Strictly Phorōnis. A surname of Io, being according to some a descendant, and according to others a sister of Phoroneus. (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 1.7.6. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Pleiades
source: Written Πλειάδες. The Pleiads, are called daughters of Atlas by Pleione (Smith's Dictionary). In Electra 468. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Pleione
source: Written Πληϊόνη. Strictly Plēionē. A daughter of Oceanus, and mother of the Pleiades by Atlas. (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 3.10.1. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Psophis
source: Written Ψωφίς. Strictly Psōphis. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Astyanassa
source: Written Ἀστυάνασσα. Said to have been a daughter of Musaeus, and a slave of Helen, and to have composed poems on immodest subjects. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Boopis
source: Written Βοῶπις. Strictly Boōpis. An epithet commonly given to Hera in the Homeric poems (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Byblis
source: Written Βυβλίς. A daughter of Miletus and Eidothea, and sister of Caunus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Caryatis
source: Written Καρυᾶτις. Strictly Karyatis. A surname of Artemis, derived from the town of Caryae in Laconia (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Chalinitis
source: Written Χαλινῖτις / Χαλινός. Strictly Khalinitis. The tamer of horses by means of the bridle, a surname of Athena, under which she had a temple at Corinth (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cirrha
source: Written Κίρρα. Strictly Kirra. A nymph from whom the town of Cirrha in Phocis was believed to have derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cnagia
source: Written Κναγία. Strictly Knagia. A surname of Artemis, derived from Cnageus, a Laconian, who accompanied the Dioseuri in their war against Aphidna, and was made prisoner (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cynosura
source: Written Κυνοσουρά. Strictly Kynosoura. An Idaean nymph and one of the nurses of Zeus, who placed her among the stars. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Daphnaea
source: Written Δαφναία / Δαφναῖος. Strictly Daphnaia. And DAPHNAEUS, surnames of Artemis and Apollo respectively, derived from δάφνη , a laurel, which was sacred to Apollo (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Derrhiatis
source: Written Δερριάτις. Strictly Derriatis. A surname of Artemis, which she derived from the town of Derrhion on the road from Sparta to Arcadia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Dindymene

name: Dionaea
source: Written Διώναια. Strictly Diōnaia. A metronymic form of Dione, and applied to her daughter Aphrodite. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Electryone
source: Written Ἠλεκτρυώνη. Strictly Ēlektryōnē. A daughter of Helios and Rhodos. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Empusa
source: Written Ἔμπουσα. Strictly Empousa. A monstrous spectre, which was believed to devour human beings (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ergane
source: Written Ἐργάνη. Strictly Erganē. Or E'RGATIS, that is, the worker, a surname of Athena, who was believed to preside over and instruct man in all kinds of arts. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Euryale
source: Written Εὐριάλη. Strictly Eurialē. The name of three mythical beings. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Evaechme
source: Written Εὐαίχμη. Strictly Euaikhmē. The name of two mythical personages. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hippia

name: Hippolyte
source: Written Ἱππούτη. Strictly Hippoutē. A daughter of Ares and Otrera, was queen of the Amazons, and a sister of Antiope and Melanippe (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849). Meaning: Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Horme
source: Written Ὁρμή. Strictly Hormē. The personification of energetic activity, who had an altar dedicated to her at Athens. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hypercheiria

name: Lacinia
source: Written Λακινία. Strictly Lakinia. A surname of Juno, under which she was worshipped in the neighbourhood of Croton, where she had a rich and famous sanctuary. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Migonitis
source: Written Μιγωνῖτις. Strictly Migōnitis. A surname of Aphrodite, derived from a place, Migonium, in or near the island of Cranne in Laconia, where the goddess had a temple. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mneme

name: Mormo
source: Written Μορμώ. Strictly Mormō. A female spectre, with which the Greeks used to frighten little children. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Morpho

name: Munychia

name: Myrrha
source: Written Μύρρα. Strictly Myrra. A daughter of Cinyras and mother of Adonis. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Oenoatis

name: Oreithyia

name: Tanagra
