Borne by 7 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 500 BC to 310 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Merops
source: Written Μέροψ. The father of Eumelus, king of the island of Cos, which he thus called after his daughter, while the inhabitants were called after him, Mero (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 2.831; Argonautica 1.975; Apollodorus 3.12.5. Borne by 6 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 998 BC to 310 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Tantalus
source: Written Τάνταλος. Strictly Tantalos. A son of Zeus by Pluto, or according to others (Smith's Dictionary). In Odyssey 11.582; Apollodorus 3.5.6; Antigone 825. Borne by 6 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 998 BC to 200 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Pylades
source: Written Πυλάδης. Strictly Pyladēs. The engraver of a beautiful gem in the Museum of the King of the Netherlands, representing an eagle, carrying a crown in its beak (Smith's Dictionary). In Libation Bearers 20; Electra 16; Electra 82. Borne by 67 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 425 BC to 325 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Antigonus
source: Written Ἀντίγονος. Strictly Antigonos. King of JUDAEA , the son of Aristobulus II. and the last of the Maccabees who sat on the royal throne (Smith's Dictionary). Borne by 619 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 500 BC to 600 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0).

name: Philoctetes
source: Written Φιλοκτήτης. Strictly Philoktētēs. A son of Poeas (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 2.718; Odyssey 3.190; Apollodorus 3.10.8. Borne by 5 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 399 BC to 200 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Proteus
source: Written Πρωτεύς. Strictly Prōteus. The prophetic old man of the sea, occurs in the earliest legends as a subject of Poseidon, and is described as seeing through the whole dept (Smith's Dictionary). In Odyssey 4.365; Apollodorus 2.1.5; Electra 1280. Borne by 5 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 375 BC to 165 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Ixion
source: Written Ἰξίων. Strictly Ixiōn. A son of Phlegyas (Smith's Dictionary). In Argonautica 3.62; Apollodorus 1.8.2; Eumenides 441. Borne by 4 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 998 BC to 31 BC. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Aristomachus
source: Written Ἀριστόμαχος. Strictly Aristomakhos. Tyrant of Argos, in the reign and under the patronage of Antigonus Gonatas (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 1.9.13; Herodotus 6.52.1. Borne by 432 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Eteoclus
source: Written Ἐτέοκλος. Strictly Eteoklos. A son of Iphis, was, according to some traditions, one of the seven heroes who went with Adrastus against Thebes (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 3.6.3; Seven against Thebes 458; Oedipus at Colonus 1316. Borne by 3 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 540 BC to 200 BC. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Phaethon
source: Written Φαέθων. Strictly Phaethōn. That is, the shining . 1. This name occurs in Homer (Smith's Dictionary). In Theogony 987; Argonautica 3.245; Apollodorus 3.14.3. Borne by 3 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 325 BC to 75 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Aegisthus
source: Written Αἴγισθος. Strictly Aigisthos. A son of Thyestes, who unwittingly begot him by his own daughter Pelopia (Smith's Dictionary). In Odyssey 1.29; Agamemnon 1436; Electra 98. Borne by 2 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 600 BC to 271 BC. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Idomeneus
source: Written Ἰδομενεύς. Of Lampsacus, a friend and disciple of Epicurus, flourished about B. C. 310 - 270 . We have no particulars of his life, save that he married (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 1.145; Odyssey 3.191; Apollodorus 3.3.1. Borne by 24 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 500 BC to 310 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Anchises
source: Written Ἀγχίσης. Strictly Ankhisēs. A son of Capys and Themis, the daughter of Ilus (Smith's Dictionary). In Theogony 1009; Iliad 2.819; Homeric Hymn 5.53. Borne by 1 person in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 488 BC to 487 BC. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Pelias
source: Written Πηλίας / Πελίας. A son of Poseidon (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 2.715; Argonautica 1.3; Apollodorus 1.9.8. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Ephialtes
source: Written Ἐφιάλτης. Strictly Ephialtēs. A Malian, who, in B. C. 480 , when Leonidas was defending the pass of Thermopylae, guided the body of Persians called the Immortals over the (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 5.385; Odyssey 11.308; Apollodorus 1.6.2. Borne by 12 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 625 BC to 155 BC. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Myrmidon
source: Written Μυρμιδών. Strictly Myrmidōn. A son of Zeus and Eurymedusa, the daughter of Cleitos, whom Zeus deceived in the disguise of an ant (Smith's Dictionary). In Argonautica 1.55; Apollodorus 1.7.3; Iphigenia in Aulis 237. Borne by 10 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 323 BC to 151 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Acastus
source: Written Ἄκαστος. Strictly Akastos. A son of Pelias, king of Iolcus, and of Anaxibia, or as others call her, Philomache (Smith's Dictionary). In Odyssey 14.336; Argonautica 1.224; Apollodorus 1.9.10. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Aeolides
source: Written Αἰολίδης. Strictly Aiolidēs. A patronymic given to the sons of Acolus, as Athamas (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 6.154; Odyssey 11.237; Works and Days 636. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Apis
source: Written Ἆπις. The Bull of Memphis, which enjoyed the highest honours as a god among the Egyptians. (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 2.1.1; Suppliants 262. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Deiphobus
source: Written Δηΐφοβος. Strictly Dēiphobos. A son of Priam and Hecabe, was next to Hector the bravest among the Trojans (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 12.94; Odyssey 4.276; Apollodorus 2.6.2. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Electryon
source: Written Ἠλεκτρύων. Strictly Ēlektryōn. A son of Perseus and Andromeda, was king of Mycenae or Mideia in Argolis. (Smith's Dictionary). In Shield 3; Argonautica 1.748; Apollodorus 2.4.5. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Enyalius
source: Written Ἐνυάλιος. Strictly Enyalios. The warlike, frequently occurs in the Iliad either as an epithet of Ares, or as a proper name instead of Ares. (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 2.651; Shield 371; Argonautica 3.322. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Inachus
source: Written Ἴναχος. Strictly Inakhos. A river god and king of Argos, is described as a son of Oceanus and Tethys (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 2.1.1; Suppliants 497; Electra 5. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Ganymedes
source: Written Γανυμήδης. Strictly Ganymēdēs. According to Homer and others, he was a son of Tros by Calirrhoe, and a brother of Ilus and Assaracus; being the most beautiful of all morta (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 5.266; Apollodorus 2.5.9; Cyclops 582. Borne by 6 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 410 BC to 310 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Melampus
source: Written Μέλαμπος / Μελάμπους. Strictly Melampous. A son of Amythaon by Eidomene, or according to others, by Aglaia or Plhodope (Smith's Dictionary). In Argonautica 1.121; Apollodorus 1.9.11; Herodotus 2.49.1. Borne by 2 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 600 BC to 300 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Asterion
source: Written Ἀστερίων / Ἀστέριος. Strictly Asteriōn. Or ASTE'RIUS (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 2.735; Argonautica 1.35; Apollodorus 1.9.9. Borne by 3 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 250 BC to 125 BC. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Hippomedon
source: Written Ἱππομέδων. Strictly Hippomedōn. A son of Aristomachus, or, according to Sophocles, of Talaus, was one of the Seven against Thebes, where he was slain during the siege by Hy (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 3.6.3; Seven against Thebes 488; Suppliants 881. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Eumolpus
source: Written Εὔμολπος. Strictly Eumolpos. That is, " the good singer," a Thracian who is described as having come to Attica either as a bard, a warrior, or a priest of Demeter and Di (Smith's Dictionary). In Homeric Hymn 2.154; Apollodorus 2.5.12; Phoenissae 854. Borne by 33 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 400 BC to 310 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Bromius
source: Written Βρόμιος. Strictly Bromios. A surname of Dionysus, which some explain by saying, that he was born during a storm of thunder and lightning (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 2.1.5; Eumenides 24; Cyclops 1. Borne by 30 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 306 BC to 400 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Astyanax
source: Written Ἀστυάναξ. The son of Hector and Andromache; his more common name was Scamandrius (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 22.500; Apollodorus 2.7.8; Trojan Women 571. Borne by 26 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 998 BC to 150 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Alcmaeon
source: Written Ἀλκμαίων. Strictly Alkmaiōn. A son of Amphiaraus and Eriphyle, and brother of Amphilochus, Eurydice, and Demonassa. (Smith's Dictionary). In Odyssey 15.248; Apollodorus 1.8.6. Borne by 1 person in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 525 BC to 475 BC. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Cycnus
source: Written Κύκνος. Strictly Kyknos. A son of Apollo by Thyria or Hyria, the daughter of Amphinomus (Smith's Dictionary). In Shield 57; Apollodorus 2.5.11; Alcestis 503. Borne by 17 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 500 BC to 310 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Demophon
source: Written Δημοφῶν / Δημοφόων. Strictly Dēmophōn. One of the two generals sent from Athens by a decree of the people, according to Diodorus, to aid the Thebans who were in arms for the recov (Smith's Dictionary). In Homeric Hymn 2.248; Heracleidae 115. Borne by 134 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Tlepolemus
source: Written Τληπόλεμος. Strictly Tlēpolemos. A son of Heracles by Astyoche, the daughter of Phylas (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 2.653; Apollodorus 2.7.6. Borne by 100 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 425 BC to 310 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Nauplius
source: Written Ναύπλιος. Strictly Nauplios. A son of Poseidon and Amymone, of Argos, a famous navigator, and father of Proetus and Damastor (Smith's Dictionary). In Argonautica 1.134; Apollodorus 2.1.5; Helen 767. Borne by 9 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 375 BC to 100 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Aegialeus
source: Written Αἰγιαλεύς. Strictly Aigialeus. A son of Adrastus and Amphithea or Demoanassa. (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 1.8.6; Suppliants 1216; Herodotus 5.68.2. Borne by 6 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 375 BC to 300 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Calydon
source: Written Καλύδων / Καλυδών. Strictly Kalydōn. A son of Aetolus and Pronoe, married to Aeolia, by whom he became the father of Epicaste and Protogeneia (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 2.640; Argonautica 1.190; Apollodorus 1.7.7. Borne by 6 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 395 BC to 310 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Euryalus
source: Written Εὐρύαλος. Strictly Euryalos. A son of Mecisteus, is mentioned by Apollodorus among the Argonauts, and was one of the Epigoni who took and destroyed Thebes. (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 2.565; Odyssey 8.115; Apollodorus 1.8.5. Borne by 5 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 675 BC to 223 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Aristocrates
source: Written Ἀριστοκράτης. Strictly Aristokratēs. An Athenian of wealth and influence (Smith's Dictionary). In Herodotus 6.73.2. Borne by 588 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Lysimachus
source: Written Λυσίμαχος. Strictly Lysimakhos. King of Thrace (Smith's Dictionary). In Herodotus 8.79.1. Borne by 533 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Talthybius
source: Written Ταλθύβιος. Strictly Talthybios. The herald of Agumenmon at Troy. (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 1.320; Hecuba 487; Herodotus 7.134.1. Borne by 4 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 279 BC to 100 BC. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Leucippus
source: Written Λεύκιππος. Strictly Leukippos. A Grecian philosopher, who is on all hands admitted to have been the founder of the atomic theory of the ancient philosophy (Smith's Dictionary). In Homeric Hymn 3.212; Apollodorus 1.9.5. Borne by 45 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Thersites
source: Written Θερσίτης. Strictly Thersitēs. A son of Agrius, the most ugly and most impudent talker among the Greeks at Troy (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 2.212; Apollodorus 1.8.6; Philoctetes 442. Borne by 2 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Aristagoras
source: Written Ἀρισταγόρας. Of Miletus, brother-in-law and cousin of Histiaeus, was left by him, on his occupation of Myrcinus and during his stay at the Persian court, (Smith's Dictionary). In Herodotus 5.30.3. Borne by 256 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Bias
source: Written Βίας. Of Priene in Ionia, is always reckoned among the Seven Sages, and is mentioned by Dicaearchus (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 13.691; Apollodorus 1.9.11. Borne by 24 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 625 BC to 310 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Cecrops
source: Written Κέκροψ. Strictly Kekrops. According to Apollodorus the first king of Attica, which derived from him its name Cecropia, having previously borne the name of Acte (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 3.14.1; Ion 272; Herodotus 7.141.3. Borne by 1 person in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 400 BC to 300 BC. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Polyidus
source: Written Πολύϊδος. Strictly Polyidos. A dithyrambic poet of the most flourishing period of the later Athenian dithyramb, and also skilful as a painter, was contemporary with Phil (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 13.663; Apollodorus 3.3.1. Borne by 19 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 479 BC to 310 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Eumenes
source: Written Εὐμένης. Strictly Eumenēs. Of CARDIA , secretary to Alexander the Great, and after his death one of the most distinguished generals among his successors (Smith's Dictionary). In Herodotus 8.93.1. Borne by 158 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Actor
source: Written Ἄκτωρ. Strictly Aktōr. A son of Deion and Diomede, the daughter of Xuthus (Smith's Dictionary). In Argonautica 1.69; Apollodorus 1.7.3; Seven against Thebes 555. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Bellerophon
source: Written Βελλεροφῶν / Βελλεροφόντης. Strictly Bellerophōn. Or BELLEROPHON, properly called Hipponous, was a son of the Corinthian king, Glaucus and Eurymede, and a grandson of Sisyphus. (Smith's Dictionary). In Theogony 325; Iliad 6.155; Apollodorus 1.9.3. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Erichthonius
source: Written Ἐριχθόνιος. Strictly Erikhthonios. There can be little doubt but that the names Erichthonius and Erechtheus are identical; but whether the two heroes mentioned by Plato, Hygin (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 20.219; Apollodorus 3.12.2; Ion 21. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Maenalus
source: Written Μαίναλος. Strictly Mainalos. The name of two mythical personages, the one a son of Lycaon, and founder of the Arcadian town of Maenalus (Smith's Dictionary). In Argonautica 1.770; Apollodorus 3.8.1; Phoenissae 1162. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Minyas
source: Written Μινύας. A son of Chryses, and the ancestral hero of the race of the Minyans; but the accounts of his genealogy vary very much in the different tradi (Smith's Dictionary). In Argonautica 1.229; Apollodorus 2.4.11; Heracles 50. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Nympiiodorus
source: Written Νυμφόδωρος. Strictly Nymphodōros. A Greek physician, who must have lived in or before the third century B. C., as he is mentioned by Heracleides of Tarentum (Smith's Dictionary). In Herodotus 7.137.3. Borne by 99 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 500 BC to 300 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Oedipus
source: Written Οἰδίπους. Strictly Oidipous. The son of Lains and Iocaste of Thebes (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 3.5.7; Antigone 167; Phoenissae 50. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Phlegyas
source: Written Φλέγυας. A king of the La pithae, a son of Ares and Chryse, the daughter of Halmus, succeeded Eteocles, who died without issue, in the government of  (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 13.302; Homeric Hymn 16.3; Apollodorus 3.5.5. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Pleuron
source: Written Πλευρών. Strictly Pleurōn. A son of Aetolus and Pronoe, and brother of Calydon, was married to Xanthippe, by whom he became the father of Agenor, Sterope, Stratonice,  (Smith's Dictionary). In Iliad 2.639; Apollodorus 1.7.7; Trachiniae 7. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Rhoecus
source: Written Ῥοῖκος. Strictly Rhoikos. The son of Phileas or Philaeus, of Samos, an architect and statuary, belonging to the earliest period in the history of Greek art, is mentio (Smith's Dictionary). In Apollodorus 3.9.2; Herodotus 3.60.4. Borne by 9 people in the Lexicon of Greek Personal Names, 600 BC to 35 AD. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); LGPN (CC BY 4.0); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Tityus
source: Written Τιτυός. Strictly Tityos. A son of Gaea, or of Zeus and Elara, the daughter of Orchomenus, was a giant in Euboea, and the father of Europa. (Smith's Dictionary). In Odyssey 7.324; Argonautica 1.181; Apollodorus 1.4.1. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849); Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: Caractacus
source: Written Καράτακος / Καταράκατος. Strictly Karatakos. Was a king of the British tribe of the Silures, and by various prosperous enterprises had raised himself above all the other British chiefs (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Carphyllides
source: Written Καρφυλλίδης. Strictly Karphyllidēs. A Greek poet, of whom there are extant two elegant epigrams in the Greek Anthology. The name of the author of the second epigram is sometime (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cenchrias
source: Written Κεγχρίας. Strictly Kenkhrias. A son of Poseidon and Peirene, was killed accidentally by Artemis (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cercyon
source: Written Κερκύων. Strictly Kerkyōn. A son of Poseidon by a daughter of Amphictyon, and accordingly a halfbrother of Triptolemus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cersobleptes
source: Written Κερσοβλέπτης. Strictly Kersobleptēs. Was son of Cotys, king of Thrace, on whose death in B. C. 358 he inherited the kingdom in conjunction with Berisades and Amadocus, who were  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Christodorus
source: Written Χριστόδωρος. Strictly Khristodōros. A Greek poet of Coptus in Egypt, was the son of Paniscus, and flourished in the reign of Anastasius I., A. D. 491-518. Works Christodorus is (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cleomyttades
source: Written Κλεομυττάδης. Strictly Kleomyttadēs. The sixth of the family of the Asclepiadae, the son of Crisamis I. and the father of Theodorus I., who lived probably in the tenth century B (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cnossus
source: Written Κνωσσός. Strictly Knōssos. The author of a work on the geography of Asia quoted by the Scholiast on Apollonius Rhodius (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Colias
source: Written Κωλιάς. Strictly Kōlias. A surname of Aphrodite, who had a statue on the Attic promontory of Colias. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Concolitanus
source: Written Κογκολίτανος. Strictly Konkolitanos. A king of the Gallic people called Gaesati, and colleague of Aneroestus, together with whom he made war against the Romans, B. C. 225 . In t (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cyamites
source: Written Κυαμίτης. Strictly Kyamitēs. The hero of beans, a mysterious being, who had a small sanctuary on the road from Athens to Eleusis (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cyathus
source: Written Κύαθος. Strictly Kyathos. The youthful cup-bearer of Oeneus, was killed by Heracles on account of a fault committed in the discharge of his duty (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Cynaegeirus
source: Written Κυναίγειρος. Strictly Kynaigeiros. Son of Euphorion and brother of the poet Aeschylus, distinguished himself by his valour at the battle of Marathon, B. C. 490 . According to  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Decatephorus
source: Written Δεκατήφορος. Strictly Dekatēphoros. That is, the god to whom the tenth part of the booty is dedicated, was a surname of Apollo at Megara (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Dendrites
source: Written Δενδρῖτης. Strictly Dendritēs. The god of the tree, a surname of Dionysus, which has the same import as Dasyllius, the giver of foliage. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Dyrrhachius
source: Written Δυρράχιος. Strictly Dyrrakhios. A son of Poseidon and Melissa, from whom the town of Dyrrachium derived its name; for formerly it was called Epidamnus, after the father of  (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Echephyllides
source: Written Ἐχεφυλλίδης. Strictly Ekhephyllidēs. A grammarian or historian, who is mentioned by Stephanus of Byzantium, and by the Scholiast on Plato's Phaedon (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Echetlus
source: Written Ἔχετλος. Strictly Ekhetlos. A mysterious being, about whom the following tradition was current at Athens (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ellops
source: Written Ἔλλοψ. A son of Ion or Tithonus, from whom Ellopia in Euboea derived its name. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Elymus
source: Written Ἔλυμος. Strictly Elymos. A Trojan, a natural son of Anchises and a brother of Eryx. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Enarephorus
source: Written Ἐναρηφόρος. Strictly Enarēphoros. A son of Hippocoön, was a most passionate suitor of Helen, when she was yet quite young (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ephorus
source: Written Ἔφορος. Strictly Ephoros. Of Cumae, a celebrated Greek historian, was, according to Suidas, to whom we are indebted for our information respecting his life, a son eit (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Epibaterius
source: Written Ἐπιβατήριος. Strictly Epibatērios. The god who conducts men on board a ship, a surname of Apollo, under which Diomedes on his return from Troy built him a temple at Troezene. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Epiceleustus
source: Written Ἐπικέλευστος. Strictly Epikeleustos. A native of Crete, who lived probably in the second or first century B. C. He is mentioned by Erotianus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Erythrus
source: Written Ἔρυθρος. Strictly Erythros. A son of Leucon, and grandson of Athamas (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Gobryas
source: Written Γωβρύας. Strictly Gōbryas. A noble Assyrian, who, in Xenophon's Cyropaedeia, goes over to Cyrus, and renders him various important services. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Gynaecothoenas
source: Written Γυναικοθοίνας. Strictly Gynaikothoinas. That is, " the god feasted by women," a surname of Ares at Tegea (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Harpalus
source: Written Ἅρπαλος. Strictly Harpalos. A Macedonian, son of Machatas. who belonged to the family of the princes of Elymiotis, and nephew of Philip, king, of Macedon, the latter ha (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Harpocration
source: Written Ἁρποκρατίων. Strictly Harpokratiōn. Of Argos, a Platonic philosopher and a friend of J. Caesar (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hasdrubal
source: Written Ἀσδρούβας. Strictly Asdroubas. According to Gesenius (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hebdomagetes
source: Written Ἑβδομαγέτης. Strictly Hebdomagetēs. A surname of Apollo, which was derived, according to some, from the fact of sacrifices being offered to him on the seventh of every month, t (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hegesandridas
source: Written Ἡγησανδμιδας. Strictly Hēgēsandmidas. Or AGESA'NDRIDAS, son of an Hegesander or Agesander, perhaps the same who is mentioned (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hegesidemus
source: Written Ἡγησίδημος. Strictly Hēgēsidēmos. An author of uncertain date, quoted by Pliny. The reference sees to be to an historical work, but even this is not certain. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hegesigonus
source: Written Ἠγησίγονος. Strictly Ēgēsigonos. A Greek writer, perhaps an historian, of uncertain country and date (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Heracleodorus
source: Written Ἡρακλεόδωρος. Strictly Hērakleodōros. A disciple of Platto, who, after being for some time under the instruction of that philosopher, became negligent, and gave himself up to idl (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hermaphroditus
source: Written Ἑρμαφρόδιτος. Strictly Hermaphroditos. The name is compounded of Hermes and Aphrodite, and is synonymous with ἀνδρογύνης , γύνανδρος , ἡμίανδρος , &c (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hiempsal
source: Written Ἱεμψάλας. Strictly Hiempsalas. Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hippalcmus
source: Written Ἵππαλκμος. Strictly Hippalkmos. The name of two mythical personages, the one a son of Pelops and Hippodameia, and the other an Argonaut. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hipposthenes
source: Written Ἱπποσθένης / Ἱπποθόωντος. Strictly Hipposthenēs. Two or three Pythagorean philosophers of this name are mentioned. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hyacinthus
source: Written Ὑάκινθος. Strictly Hyakinthos. The youngest son of the Spartan king Amyclas and Diomede (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hyas
source: Written Ὕας. The name of the father and brother of the Hyades. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hyes
source: Written Ὕης. Strictly Hyēs. The moist or fertilising god, occurs like Hyetius, as a surname of Zeus, as the sender of rain. Under the name of Hyetius, the god had an al (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Hypatodorus
source: Written Ὑπατόδωρος. Strictly Hypatodōros. A statuary of Thebes (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ibycus
source: Written Ἴβυκος. Strictly Ibykos. The fifth lyric poet in the Alexandrine canon, was a native of Rhegium (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ichthyocentaurus
source: Written Ἰχθυοκένταυρος. Strictly Ikhthyokentauros. That is, a fish-centaur, or a particular kind of Triton (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lampter
source: Written Λαμπτήρ. Strictly Lamptēr. I. e. the shining or torch-bearer, a surname of Dionysus, under which he was worshipped at Pellene in Achaia, where a festival called λαμπτή (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lar
source: Written Λάρας / Λάρος. Strictly Laras. Or LARS (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lityerses
source: Written Λιτυέρσης. Strictly Lityersēs. A natural son of Midas, lived at Celaenae in Phrygia, engaged in rural pursuits, and hospitably received all strangers that passed his house (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Lycophronides
source: Written Λυκοφρυνίδης. Strictly Lykophrynidēs. A lyric poet, quoted by Clearchus, the disciple of Aristotle. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Maeonides
source: Written Μαιόνιδης. Strictly Maionidēs. Properly a son of Maeon, the husband of Dindyme, who was the mother of Cybele, or a native of Maeonia, which was the ancient name of a porti (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Manaechmus
source: Written Μάναιχμος. Strictly Manaikhmos. Or MENAECHMUS (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mezentius
source: Written Μεσέντιος. Strictly Mesentios. A mythical king of the Tyrrhenians or Etruscans, at Caere or Agylla, and father of Lausus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Misenus
source: Written Μισηνός. Strictly Misēnos. A companion of Odysseus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mithrobarzanes
source: Written Μιθροβαρζάνης. Strictly Mithrobarzanēs. Father-in-law of Datames, with whom he joined in his revolt from the Persian king ; but afterwards despairing of his cause, went over to Art (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mixoparthenos
source: Written Μιχοπάρθενος. Strictly Mikhoparthenos. I. e. half maiden, a surname of the Erinnyes or Furies. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mnasalcas
source: Written Μνασάλκας. Strictly Mnasalkas. An epigrammatic poet, a native of a village or township in the territory of Sicyon called Platacae (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mnemarchus
source: Written Μνήμαρχος. Strictly Mnēmarkhos. Is the name sometimes given to the father of Pythagoras; but his proper name is Mnesarchus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Mnesaechmus
source: Written Μνήσαιχμος. Strictly Mnēsaikhmos. An Athenian orator of the time of Demosthenes, is also called Menesaechmus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Myiagrus
source: Written Μυίαγρος. Strictly Myiagros. Or MYIODES, that is, the fly-catcher, is the name of a hero, who was invoked at Aliphera, at the festival of Athena, as the protector agains (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ninyas
source: Written Νινύας. The son of Ninus and Semiramis, is spoken of under SEMIRAMIS. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Oenomarchus
source: Written Οἰνόμαρχος. Strictly Oinomarkhos. Of Andros, one of the numerous pupils of Herodes Atticus. did not possess any great celebrity, and was fond of the florid style of eloquence (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Oenotropae
source: Written Οἰνοτρόπαι. Strictly Oinotropai. That is, the changers of or into wine, was the name of the three or four daughters of king Anius in Delos, because they had received from Di (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Oenotrus
source: Written Οἴνωτρος. Strictly Oinōtros. The youngest son of Lvcaon who emigrated with a colony from Arcadia to Italy, and called the district in which he settled, after himself, Oe (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Oeoclus
source: Written Οἴοκλος. Strictly Oioklos. A son of Poseidon by Ascra, who in conjunction with the Aloadae, is said to have built the town of Ascra in Boeotia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Oetosyrus
source: Written Οἰτόσυρος. Strictly Oitosyros. The name of a Scythian divinity whom Herodotus identifies with the Greek Apollo. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Olynthus
source: Written Ὄλυνθος. Strictly Olynthos. A son of Heracles and Bolbe, from whom the Thracian town of Olynthus, and the river Olynthus near the Chalcidian town of Apollonia, were bel (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Onasimedes
source: Written Ὀνασιμήδης. Strictly Onasimēdēs. A statuary, who made a statue of Dionysus, of solid bronze, which Pausanias saw at Thebes. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Opus
source: Written Ὀποῦς. Strictly Opous. A son of Zeus and Protogeneia, the daughter of Deucalion, was king of the Epeians, and father of Cambyse or Protogeneia. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Ornodopantes
source: Written Ὀρνοδοπάντης. Strictly Ornodopantēs. A Persian satrap, whom Bibulus persuaded in B. C. 50 to revolt from Orodes, the Parthian king, and proclaim Pacorus as king. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Oroebantius
source: Written Ὀροιβάντιος. Strictly Oroibantios. Of Troezene, an ancient epic poet, whose poems were said by the Troezenians to be more ancient than those of Homer. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Orontobates
source: Written Ὀροντοβάτης. Strictly Orontobatēs. A Persian, who married the daughter of Pixodarus, the usurping satrap of Caria, and was sent by the king to succeed him (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Orthrus
source: Written Ὄρθρος. Strictly Orthros. The dog of Geryones, who was begotten by Typhon and Echidna. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Othryoneus
source: Written Ὀθρψονεύς. Strictly Othrpsoneus. An ally of king Priam, from Cabesos, who sued for the hand of Cassandra, and promised in return to drive the Greeks from Troy, but was slain (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Palaemon
source: Written Παλαίμων. Strictly Palaimōn. Signifies the wrestler, as in the surname of Heracles in Lycophron; but it also occurs as a proper name of several mythical personages. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Palaeologus
source: Written Παλαιολόγος. Strictly Palaiologos. The name of an illustrious Byzantine family, of which there are said to have been descendants still existing in the 17th century (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Palaestinus
source: Written Παλαιστῖνος. Strictly Palaistinos. A son of Poseidon and father of Haliacmon (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Palinurus
source: Written Παλινοῦρος. Strictly Palinouros. The son of Jasus, and helmsman of Aeneas (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pamprepius
source: Written Παμπρέπιος. Strictly Pamprepios. An Egyptian, eminent for his literary attainments and his political influence, in the latter half of the fifth century (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pandemos
source: Written Πάνδημος. Strictly Pandēmos. I. e. "commllon to all the people," occurs as a surname of Aphrodite, and that in a twofold sense, first describing her as the goddess of lo (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pandionidae
source: Written Πανδιονίδαι. Strictly Pandionidai. A patronymic of Pandion, i. e. the sons of Pandion, who, after their father's death, returned from Megara to Athens, and expelled the Metion (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Panomphaeus
source: Written Πανομφαῖος. Strictly Panomphaios. I. e. the author of all signs and omens, occurs as a surname of Helios (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phlegethon
source: Written Φλεγέθων. Strictly Phlegethōn. I. e. the flaming, a river in the lower world, is described as a son of Cocytus; butheis more commonly called Pyriphlegethon. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phleon
source: Written Φλέων. Strictly Phleōn. I. e. the giver of plenty, is a surname of Dionysus, describing the god as promoting the fretility of plants and trees. A similar surname of (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Phratapiiernes
source: Written Φραταφέρνης. Strictly Phrataphernēs. A Persian who held the government of Parthia and Hyrcania, under Dareius Codomannus, and joined that monarch with the contingents from the p (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Picus
source: Written Πῖκος. Strictly Pikos. A Latin prophetic divinity, is described as a son of Saturnus or Sterculus, as the husband of Canens, and the father of Faunus (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Polysperchon
source: Written Πολυσπέρχων. Strictly Polysperkhōn. Son of Simmias, a Macedonian of the province of Stymphaea, and a distinguished officer in the service of Alexander the Great (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Polystephanus
source: Written Πολυστέφανος. Strictly Polystephanos. A Greek writer, possessed no small reputation, but his writings were full of incredible tales. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Proaeresius
source: Written Προαιρέσιος. Strictly Proairesios. Distinguished teacher of rhetoric, was a native of Armenia, born about A. D. 276 , of good connections, though poor (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Procrustes
source: Written Προκρούστης. Strictly Prokroustēs. That is, "the Stretcher," is a surname of the famous robber Polypemon or Damastes (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Psilas
source: Written Ψιλᾶς. I. e. "the giver of wings," or "the unbearded," a surname of Dionysus, under which he was worshipped at Amyclae. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pteras
source: Written Πτέρας. Of Delphi, a mythical artist, who was said to have built the second temple of Apollo at Delphi (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Pyriphlegethon
source: Written Πυριθλεγέθων. Strictly Pyrithlegethōn. Flaming with fire, is the name of one of the rivers in the lower world. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Rhampsinitus
source: Written Ῥαμφίνιτος. Strictly Rhamphinitos. Called Rhemphis by Diodorus, one of the ancient kings of Egypt, is said to have succeeded Proteus, and to have been himself succeeded by Che (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sanchuniathon
source: Written Σαλχουνιάθων. Strictly Salkhouniathōn. An ancient Phoenician writer, whose works were translated into Greek by Philon Byblius, who lived in the latter half of the first century of (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sandrocottus
source: Written Σανδρόκοττος. Strictly Sandrokottos. An Indian king at the time of Seleucus Nicator, ruled over the powerful nation of the Gangaridae and Prasii on the banks of the Ganges (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sardanapalus
source: Written Σαρδανάπαλος. Strictly Sardanapalos. The last king of the Assyrian empire of Ninus or Nineveh, according to Ctesias (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sarus
source: Written Σάρος. Strictly Saros. A Gothic commander in the Roman army, in the time of Arcadius and Honorius (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Satibarzanes
source: Written Σατιβαρζάνης. Strictly Satibarzanēs. A Persian, was satrap of Aria under Dareius III. In B. C. 330 , Alexander the Great, marching through the borders of Aria on his way from Hy (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Schedius
source: Written Σχέδιυς. Strictly Skhedius. A son of Iphitus by Hippolyte, commanded the Phocians in the war against Troy, along with his brother Epistrophus. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sophagasenus
source: Written Σοφαγασῆνος. Strictly Sophagasēnos. A king of India, with whom Antiochus the Great is said to have renewed an alliance, and from whom he obtained some elephants, when he crosse (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Sphettus
source: Written Σφηττός. Strictly Sphēttos. A son of Troezen. who, with his brother Anaphlystus, emigrated from Troezene to Attica, where two demi were named after him. (Smith's Dictionary). Sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography and Mythology (1849).

name: Spithridates
